title: Inference and serving
lead: What happens when a model answers: why output tokens are slow and input tokens are not, how memory decides how many users a GPU can hold, what quantisation and speculative decoding buy, and how to size, measure and run the serving of a model you own at a latency and cost you can predict.
prerequisites: Module 06: attention, multi-head and grouped-query attention, RoPE, the modern decoder block, counting parameters and FLOPs (2·N_matmul FLOPs per token plus attention, with memory counted from all N parameters), and the KV cache as introduced there

Module 07: the language-modelling objective and perplexity, tokenisation, decoding and sampling (greedy, temperature, top-p), the context window, cost from first principles, and the running case study's model, workload and assumed prices
Module 08: floating-point formats for training (fp32, bf16, fp16, fp8), memory accounting, and the idea of tensor and pipeline parallelism
Module 09: chat templates, LoRA and QLoRA, evaluation suites, and the running case study's post-training, which ends with the merged model this module quantises and serves
Mathematics: operation counts of matrix-vector and matrix-matrix products; discrete probability (sums over a distribution, expectations, the finite geometric series)
Python and PyTorch at the level of the Module 02 and Module 06 labs
outcomes: Derive the arithmetic intensity of matrix-vector and matrix-matrix products and use the roofline model to say whether prefill or decode is compute-bound or bandwidth-bound on a given accelerator.

Estimate time to first token and time per output token for any model on any accelerator from parameter count, bytes per weight, FLOP/s and memory bandwidth, and explain why batching raises decode throughput but not one user's speed.
Derive the KV-cache size 2·L·n_kv·d_head·b·T·B, compute it from a model's configuration file, and turn it into the number of concurrent sequences a GPU can hold.
Explain continuous batching, chunked prefill, paged attention and prefix caching, and predict from a workload or a prompt layout whether each will help.

Quantise a weight matrix to int8 and int4 with absmax and zero-point schemes at per-tensor, per-channel and group-wise granularity, count the bits per weight including scales, measure the effect on perplexity, and explain what GPTQ, AWQ and SmoothQuant add.

Derive the speculative-sampling acceptance rule, prove that it leaves the target model's output distribution unchanged, and compute the expected speed-up from the acceptance rate, the draft length and the draft's cost.

Size the serving of the case-study 9.5B model at 4 bits on a 24 GB GPU: weights, cache budget, concurrency, latency at low and at full load, throughput, cost per million tokens, and what the real utilisation does to that cost.
Define TTFT, TPOT, inter-token latency, throughput, goodput and percentiles; design an open-loop load test; set an SLO and find the request rate a server sustains under it.

Specify the reliability measures of a self-hosted model (versioning by hash, provenance, health checks, timeouts, retries, exercised fallbacks, metering, privacy-preserving logging) and state the limits of determinism.
Choose hardware and a serving engine for a workload with dated, conservative reasoning, reading a datasheet for the three numbers that matter.

sections.title: Two phases: prefill and decode
sections.purpose: Show that answering a prompt is one parallel pass over the prompt followed by one pass per output token, and estimate the time of each from FLOPs and bytes.
must_cover: The generation loop: prompt tokens -> forward pass -> logits at the last position -> sample (Module 07) -> append -> repeat until an end-of-sequence token, a stop string or max_tokens.

Prefill: all T_p prompt positions in one forward pass, in parallel; it writes every layer's keys and values into the KV cache and yields the first output token; at inference the logits are needed only at the last position.
Decode: one new position per forward pass; the new token's query attends to the cached keys and values; every weight is read from memory once per step, whatever the batch.

FLOPs, by Module 06's convention, recalled in one paragraph with a link (Module 06 derives it; do not re-derive the attention term): memory counts all N parameters; FLOPs count N_matmul, the parameters that take part in matrix multiplications (all but the input embedding table, which is a lookup). A forward pass costs 2·N_matmul FLOPs per token plus 4·L·d·t of attention at context t (d = n_h·d_head). Summed over a causal prompt, Σ_{t=1}^{T_p} 4·L·d·t = 2·L·d·T_p(T_p + 1) ≈ 2·L·d·T_p², so prefill FLOPs ≈ 2·N_matmul·T_p + 2·L·d·T_p²; write this one sum out. For the case study N = 9.55×10⁹ and N_matmul = 8.93×10⁹, so a token costs 1.79×10¹⁰ FLOPs before attention; 2N with the total count (1.91×10¹⁰) overestimates by 7% and may appear only labelled as such.
Bytes per decode step: the weights plus this sequence's cache (147,456·t bytes for the case-study model at context t, derived in s3).

The time model used throughout the module: TTFT ≈ queueing + prefill FLOPs / (MFU · peak FLOP/s); TPOT ≈ bytes per step / bandwidth; end-to-end latency E2E = TTFT + (n_out − 1)·TPOT. State explicitly that an MFU (model FLOPs utilisation) of 50% for prefill is an assumption used for every estimate in the module, and that decode estimates use peak bandwidth. State the units once here: decimal throughout (kB = 10³ B, GB = 10⁹ B, TB/s = 10¹² B/s); Modules 03 and 06 use binary units, so a quantity that also appears there is given in both forms (s3).

Why input tokens are cheap and output tokens dear: prefill turns thousands of tokens into one read of the weights; decode spends one read per token. This is the mechanism behind output tokens being priced above input tokens (link Module 07's cost section; do not re-derive prices).

Introduce the running case study in two or three sentences, as hypothetical: the open-weight bilingual (English-Chinese) model of about 9.5B parameters (N = 9.55×10⁹) chosen in Module 07 and adapted in Modules 08 and 09 to draft and check safety-case arguments for the pressure-relief system of a reactor vessel; this module serves the artifact Module 09 hands over, its LoRA adapter merged into bf16 weights, quantised to a 5.5 GB 4-bit file, for requests of about 4,000 tokens in and 2,000 out, about 2,000 a day. Its configuration and sizing are in s11.
worked_examples: Prefill of a 2,000-token prompt on the case-study model (N_matmul = 8.93×10⁹, L = 36, d = 4,096): matmuls 2 × 8.93×10⁹ × 2,000 = 3.57×10¹³ FLOPs (the source's 3.6×10¹³, rounded); attention 2 × 36 × 4,096 × 2,000² = 1.18×10¹² (3.3% of the matmul term); total 3.69×10¹³. On an H100-class GPU (989 TFLOP/s dense bf16, datasheet) at the assumed 50% MFU: 75 ms. On a 24 GB consumer card (165 TFLOP/s dense fp16 with fp32 accumulation, the RTX 4090's published figure) at 50%: 0.45 s.

Decode on the 24 GB card (about 1.0 TB/s), weights only, the source's first estimate: 5.5 GB / 1.0 TB/s = 5.5 ms per token, about 180 tokens/s. Refinement: the input embedding table is not read in full (one row per token), so about 4.9 GB is read per step (the 5.53 GB file less its 0.62 GB 8-bit embedding), but kernels reach roughly 85% of peak bandwidth: 4.9 GB / 0.85 TB/s = 5.8 ms. The two corrections nearly cancel, so the module uses the 5.5 GB file at peak bandwidth, plus the sequence's cache, as the bound.

A 500-token answer to the 2,000-token prompt on the 24 GB card: the mean context during decode is 2,250 tokens, whose cache adds 0.33 GB, so TPOT ≈ (5.5 + 0.33) GB / 1.0 TB/s = 5.83 ms and E2E ≈ 0.45 + 499 × 0.00583 = 3.36 s, of which 87% is decode. Doubling the prompt to 4,000 tokens raises the prefill to 7.61×10¹³ FLOPs and TTFT to 0.92 s, but changes TPOT only through the larger cache (6.13 ms at a mean context of 4,250).
Attention at long context: at T = 32,768 the causal attention term (3.17×10¹⁴ FLOPs) is 54% of the matmul term (5.85×10¹⁴), so long-context prefill is no longer '2·N_matmul per token'.

figures.description: Timeline of one request on the 24 GB card: a wide prefill block (2,000 prompt tokens processed together, 0.45 s, labelled 'compute-bound') followed by a train of thin decode steps (about 5.8 ms each, labelled 'bandwidth-bound'); brackets marking TTFT, TPOT and end-to-end latency (3.4 s for 500 output tokens). Beneath, paired bars for each phase: prefill 3.7×10¹³ FLOPs and 5.5 GB of weights read; one decode step 1.9×10¹⁰ FLOPs (1.79×10¹⁰ in matmuls plus 1.2×10⁹ of attention at a 2,000-token context) and about 5.8 GB read (weights plus cache).

checks: Doubling the prompt length roughly doubles TTFT. What does it do to TPOT? -> Almost nothing: TPOT is set by the bytes read per step, dominated by the 5.5 GB of weights; 2,000 more tokens add 0.29 GB of cache, about 5% more bytes.

Two GPUs have the same 1 TB/s of bandwidth but 165 and 989 TFLOP/s. Which decodes a single sequence faster? -> Neither, to first order: a decode step's 1.9×10¹⁰ FLOPs take about 0.1 ms on the slower card, while reading 5.5 GB takes 5.5 ms on both.

sections.title: The roofline model: compute-bound and bandwidth-bound
sections.purpose: Give the reader one diagram and one ratio, arithmetic intensity against the ridge point, that decide whether an operation is limited by compute or by memory bandwidth, and use it to explain why batching helps decode.
must_cover: Definitions: arithmetic intensity I = FLOPs performed / bytes moved between off-chip memory and the compute units; attainable throughput P(I) = min(P_peak, I·BW); ridge point I* = P_peak / BW (Williams, Waterman and Patterson 2009). Below I* an operation is bandwidth-bound, above it compute-bound.

Derive the matrix-vector case: y = Wx with W ∈ R^{m×n} at b bytes per element: FLOPs 2mn; bytes b(mn + n + m); I = 2mn / (b(mn + m + n)) ≈ 2/b. bf16: ≈1 FLOP/byte; int8 weights: ≈2; 4-bit weights with fp16 activations: ≈4.

Derive the matrix-matrix case with B columns (B tokens processed together): Y = WX with X ∈ R^{n×B}: FLOPs 2mnB; bytes b(mn + nB + mB); I = 2mnB / (b(mn + nB + mB)). For m = n = d: I = 2dB / (b(d + 2B)); for B ≪ d, I ≈ 2B/b; for B ≫ d, I → d/b.

Ridge points from published dense figures: H100 SXM 989 TFLOP/s / 3.35 TB/s = 295 FLOP/byte; the 24 GB consumer card 165 / 1.0 ≈ 165. Decode at batch 1 sits two orders of magnitude below the ridge; the prefill of thousands of tokens sits above it. The full table is in s4.

Why batching helps decode: B sequences in one step share a single read of the weights, so the step time stays nearly flat until 2B/b reaches the ridge: bf16 on the H100: B ≈ 295; 4-bit weights on the 24 GB card: 4B = 165, so B ≈ 41.

Decode attention does not batch: each sequence reads its own cache. Per layer, FLOPs 4·n_h·d_head·t and bytes 2·n_kv·d_head·t·b, so I = 2(n_h/n_kv)/b: 4 FLOP/byte for the case study (group size 4, bf16) whatever B is. Batching amortises the weights, never the KV cache; at long contexts this caps the gain (s5). This refines the source's statement that throughput scales almost linearly with the batch until compute becomes the limit: that holds for short contexts only.
Efficiency measures to report: MFU = achieved model FLOP/s ÷ peak (for prefill); MBU (memory-bandwidth utilisation) = achieved bytes/s ÷ peak bandwidth (for decode).

One paragraph of datasheet caution, pointing to s4: use dense figures, not 'with sparsity'; consumer cards quote fp16 with fp16 accumulation at twice the fp32-accumulate rate that most inference kernels use; bandwidth and FLOP/s are peaks.
worked_examples: Intensity of a 4,096 × 4,096 bf16 matmul as B grows: B = 1: 0.9995 ≈ 1.0; B = 16: 15.9; B = 64: 62.1; B = 256: 227.6; B = 2,048: 1,024 FLOP/byte. On the H100 (ridge 295) only the prefill-sized product is compute-bound.
Batch-1 bf16 decode on the H100: I ≈ 1, so the attainable rate is 1 × 3.35 TB/s = 3.35 TFLOP/s, 0.34% of the 989 TFLOP/s peak.

The batch at which weight traffic stops dominating: bf16 on the H100: 2B/2 = 295, B ≈ 295; 4-bit weights on the 24 GB card: 2B/0.5 = 165, B ≈ 41; for the case study's whole 5.5 GB file (which includes an 8-bit output head), the weights-only balance is B = 165×10¹² × 5.5×10⁹ / (2 × 8.93×10⁹ × 1.0×10¹²) ≈ 51, with N_matmul in the FLOPs.

A CPU measured while preparing Lab 1 (4 threads, fp32, a desktop shared with other jobs): about 12.6 GB/s for a matrix-vector product, so about 21 ms for Lab 1's 8,192 × 8,192 matrix (268 MB); almost the same time for every B from 2 to 16 (B = 1 can be faster still, because PyTorch hands a one-column product to a separate matrix-vector kernel); about 200-250 GFLOP/s at large B, so a ridge of about 15-20 FLOP/byte. Present it as one machine's measurement; the reader measures their own in Lab 1.

figures.description: Log-log roofline. x-axis: arithmetic intensity, 0.1 to 10,000 FLOP/byte; y-axis: attainable TFLOP/s. Two rooflines: H100 SXM (sloped at 3.35 TB/s, flat at 989, ridge at 295) and the 24 GB consumer card (sloped at 1.0 TB/s, flat at 165, ridge at 165). Four labelled points for a 4,096 × 4,096 bf16 matmul: decode B = 1 (I = 1.0), B = 16 (15.9), B = 256 (228), prefill of 2,048 tokens (1,024). The region left of each ridge shaded 'bandwidth-bound', right of it 'compute-bound'. A small inset: the case study's decode attention at I = 4, marked 'does not move with B'.

checks: An int8 weight-only matrix-vector product runs on a GPU whose ridge point is 200 FLOP/byte. Compute- or bandwidth-bound, and by how much? -> Intensity ≈ 2 FLOP/byte, a hundred times below the ridge: bandwidth-bound, running at about 1% of peak FLOP/s.

Why does batching 64 long-context sequences not give 64 times the throughput of one? -> The weights are read once per step for all 64, but each sequence's KV cache is read separately; at long context those reads dominate the step.

sections.title: The KV cache in depth
sections.purpose: Derive the size of the key-value cache, show that it is the number that decides concurrency, and list the ways to shrink it.
must_cover: Why caching is exact: under the causal mask the key and value at position i depend only on tokens ≤ i, so they never change once computed. At each decode step only the new token's q, k and v are computed; k and v are appended; q attends to all cached keys. Without the cache, step t recomputes t positions: Σ t = O(T²) position-forwards per sequence instead of O(T). Module 06 introduced the cache; this section owns its depth.

Derive the size: per token per layer, one key vector and one value vector for each of n_kv heads, each of d_head values, so 2·n_kv·d_head values; times L layers and b bytes per value gives 2·L·n_kv·d_head·b bytes per token; for B sequences of T tokens, M_KV = 2·L·n_kv·d_head·b·T·B.

Grouped-query attention (Module 06): n_kv key/value heads shared by n_h > n_kv query heads divide the cache by n_h/n_kv; multi-query attention (one KV head, Shazeer 2019) is the extreme; GQA (Ainslie et al. 2023) is the usual compromise. This is why the case study has 8 KV heads and not 32.

The cache against the weights: for the case study one sequence's cache equals the 5.5 GB of weights at about 37,300 tokens; at 18 sequences with 5,000 tokens of context, the cache read per decode step (13.3 GB) is 2.4 times the weight read.

Other ways to shrink the cache: sliding-window attention caps it at the window (Mistral 7B, 2023: 4,096 tokens); multi-head latent attention (DeepSeek-V2, 2024) caches a compressed latent vector per token and layer instead of full keys and values; an 8-bit cache halves it (s8); offloading to CPU memory trades capacity for the much lower bandwidth of the host link.
Implementation: a cache that grows by concatenation copies itself at every step; engines pre-allocate, and paging (s6) allocates in blocks.

Positions: with RoPE (Module 06) the new token's rotation uses its absolute position, which equals the number of tokens already cached. An off-by-one here crashes nothing and degrades quality slowly: in Lab 2 it changes the logits by about 0.03 while leaving greedy tokens unchanged, so tests must compare logits, not tokens.
worked_examples: Case-study model (L = 36, n_kv = 8, d_head = 128, bf16): 2 × 36 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 147,456 bytes per token (147 kB); 2,000 tokens: 0.29 GB; 6,000 tokens: 0.885 GB; 32,000 tokens: 4.72 GB. With 32 KV heads (multi-head attention): 589,824 bytes per token and 3.54 GB per 6,000-token sequence; with one KV head: 18,432 bytes; with an 8-bit cache: 73,728 bytes.

Published configurations (each model's config.json), bf16 cache per token: Llama-2-7B (32 layers, 32 KV heads, d_head 128, multi-head): 524,288 B (512 KiB, the figure Module 06 quotes); Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B (32 layers, 8 KV heads, d_head 128): 131,072 B; Qwen2.5-7B (28 layers, 4 KV heads, d_head 128): 57,344 B. For a 4,096-token sequence: 2.15 GB, 0.54 GB and 0.23 GB. (Do not give the SmolLM2 or Qwen2.5-0.5B figures here: they are Exercise e3.)
How many 6,000-token sequences fit in 16 GB of cache: the case study (8 KV heads) 18; the same model with multi-head attention 4.

sections.title: Hardware: the three numbers on a datasheet
sections.purpose: Read an accelerator datasheet for the three numbers that matter, memory capacity, memory bandwidth and dense compute, and turn them into concurrency, decode speed and prefill speed.
must_cover: Capacity decides the largest model and the number of concurrent sequences; bandwidth decides decode speed; dense compute decides prefill speed and large-batch throughput; across several GPUs, the interconnect decides whether tensor parallelism pays.

A dated table ('published datasheet figures, dense, no sparsity, as of 2026'): H100 SXM: 80 GB, 3.35 TB/s, 989 TFLOP/s bf16; A100 80 GB SXM: 80 GB, 2.04 TB/s, 312; L40S: 48 GB, 0.864 TB/s, 362; L4: 24 GB, 0.30 TB/s, 121; RTX 4090: 24 GB, 1.01 TB/s (the module rounds to 1.0), 165 (fp16 with fp32 accumulation); Apple M2 Ultra: up to 192 GB unified memory, 0.8 TB/s; a laptop with dual-channel DDR5-5600: 2 channels × 8 bytes × 5.6×10⁹ transfers/s = 89.6 GB/s theoretical. Derived columns: ridge point, and the decode upper bound for the case study at one 5,000-token sequence (5.5 GB of weights + 0.74 GB of cache = 6.24 GB per step).

Same memory, different speed: the L4 and the RTX 4090 both have 24 GB, so both hold the case study's 18 sequences, but the L4 decodes about 3.3 times slower (1.0/0.30 = 3.3). This corrects the source's grouping of 'a consumer or L4-class card' as one row of its sizing table.

Datasheet traps: 'with sparsity' figures are twice the dense ones; consumer cards' fp16-accumulate figures are twice the fp32-accumulate rate most inference kernels use; memory is sold in binary units (a '24 GB' card holds 24 GiB = 25.8×10⁹ bytes; the module uses decimal GB and treats the difference as margin); bandwidth and FLOP/s are peaks: plan with 70-90% of peak bandwidth and 40-60% of peak FLOP/s, then measure.

Consumer versus datacentre parts: memory size, ECC, multi-GPU interconnect, cooling and form factor, and driver licence terms that restrict datacentre use of consumer cards (check them). A 24 GB card is adequate for a 9B model at modest concurrency and is what a first deployment often runs on.

Several GPUs: tensor parallelism splits every layer across GPUs, so weights, bandwidth and compute add (two GPUs roughly halve the per-token time) at the cost of an all-reduce per layer, which needs a fast interconnect; pipeline parallelism adds capacity, not single-stream speed. Mechanics in Module 08.

CPUs and Apple silicon: decode is bandwidth-bound and tolerable (the case study on the laptop: at most 14 tokens/s, typically 7-10 achieved); prefill is compute-bound and slow: at an assumed 0.5 TFLOP/s sustained, a 4,000-token prompt (7.61×10¹³ FLOPs) takes about 150 s. Unified memory lets a laptop hold models a 24 GB card cannot. llama.cpp is the usual engine.

Other accelerators (AMD Instinct, Google TPU, Intel Gaudi, Huawei Ascend and others) and market-specific GPU variants run the same models through their own serving stacks and quantised formats; the roofline reasoning applies unchanged once the three numbers are known.

sections.title: Batching: static, dynamic and continuous
sections.purpose: Show how a server keeps the GPU busy with many sequences at once, and what each batching policy does to throughput and to each user's latency.
must_cover: Static batching: B requests padded to a common length and run together until the longest finishes; three wastes: padding, slots idle after short sequences finish, and new arrivals blocked until the whole batch ends.

Dynamic (request-level) batching: dispatch when B requests are queued or after a maximum wait τ; trades a little latency for throughput; still holds every slot until the longest output in the batch ends.

Continuous (iteration-level) batching (Orca, Yu et al. 2022): the scheduler runs once per forward iteration; finished sequences leave and waiting requests join at every step. Selective batching: the linear layers process all tokens of all sequences as one matrix; attention runs per sequence over its own cache.

Prefill-decode interference: a joining request's prefill shares the iteration, so every running sequence sees one long gap (about 0.92 s for a 4,000-token prompt on the 24 GB card). Chunked prefill (Sarathi-Serve, Agrawal et al. 2024) caps the prompt tokens per iteration and mixes them with decodes in the same forward pass, so the iteration costs max(bytes / bandwidth, FLOPs / compute) of the combined batch and the gap is bounded; the chunk must suit the GPU's compute (on the 24 GB card an iteration carrying a 512-token chunk and 17 decodes at a 5,000-token context takes about 116 ms when the chunk opens its prompt and 123 ms when 2,000 of the prompt's tokens are already cached; with a 128-token chunk, 32 and 34 ms). Disaggregation (DistServe, Zhong et al. 2024; Splitwise, Patel et al. 2024) runs prefill and decode on different GPUs and transfers the cache.

The throughput-latency trade-off in the bandwidth-bound regime: step time t(B) = (W + B·k·t̄)/BW, with W the weight bytes, k the cache bytes per token and t̄ the mean context; per-sequence speed 1/t(B) falls and aggregate speed B/t(B) rises with diminishing returns; compute binds only when (2·N_matmul·B + 4·L·d·B·t̄)/peak exceeds t(B).
Scheduler controls: maximum running sequences, maximum tokens per iteration, the cache budget for admission; when the cache runs out, preemption (s6).
worked_examples: Static versus continuous with four slots, a 20 ms step, and output lengths 100, 200, 400 and 800 tokens: static batching runs 800 steps (16 s) and uses 1,500 of 3,200 slot-steps (46.9%), 94 tokens/s; continuous batching with a queue of waiting requests refills each slot as it frees and sustains 4 / 0.02 = 200 tokens/s, 2.1 times more.

The case study on the 24 GB card at a mean context of 5,000 tokens (0.737 GB of cache per sequence): B = 1: 6.24 ms, 160 tokens/s; B = 4: 8.45 ms, 118 per sequence, 473 aggregate; B = 8: 11.4 ms, 88 / 702; B = 18: 18.8 ms, 53 / 959. Compute at B = 18 is 3.7×10¹¹ FLOPs, 2.3 ms at peak: still bandwidth-bound, because the cache reads grow with B.

Lab 3's simulator on a variable workload (prompts uniform in 2,000-6,000 tokens, outputs lognormal with median 1,500 and a mean of about 1,740 after the clip at 4,000): static batching saturates near 300 output tokens/s and, at 0.1 requests/s, already has a median TTFT of about 13 s because each batch holds the GPU until its longest request ends; continuous batching saturates near 560-590 tokens/s with a median TTFT of about 1 s at the same load (prototype values; writers use the lab's output).

sections.title: Paged attention and prefix caching
sections.purpose: Explain how serving engines allocate the cache in pages so that many sequences of unpredictable length fit, and how they reuse the cache of a shared prefix across requests.
must_cover: Why contiguous allocation wastes memory: the output length is unknown, so a naive server reserves the maximum length per request; waste comes from reserved slots never used, the unused tail of each allocation, and gaps between allocations of different sizes. Kwon et al. (2023) measured that in the systems they studied only 20.4-38.2% of cache memory held actual token states.

PagedAttention: the cache is divided into fixed-size blocks (16 tokens by default in vLLM); each sequence has a block table mapping its logical blocks to physical ones, allocated on demand as it grows; waste is at most one partly filled block per sequence; the attention kernel gathers keys and values through the block table. The analogy is virtual memory with pages.

Sharing and copy-on-write: sequences that share a prefix (parallel samples of one prompt, beam search) point to the same physical blocks, with reference counts; a shared block is copied only when one sequence must write into it.

Preemption when blocks run out: swap a sequence's blocks to CPU memory, or drop them and recompute later. Under sustained overload this churn wastes work (Lab 3 shows hundreds of preemptions past saturation).

Prefix caching: full blocks are identified by a hash of their tokens and of everything before them; a new request whose token prefix matches reuses those blocks and skips their prefill; unreferenced blocks are evicted least-recently-used. SGLang's RadixAttention (Zheng et al. 2024) keeps a radix tree over cached token sequences, which also serves multi-turn chat and agent loops.

What breaks a hit: any change early in the prompt (a timestamp, a user name, a reordered tool list), a different rendering by the chat template, a prefix that ends mid-block (only full blocks are cached), eviction under memory pressure, a different adapter. Layout rule: stable content first (system prompt, tool definitions, shared documents), variable content last.

Hosted APIs expose the same mechanism as prompt caching (Module 07 prices it from the client's side; link, do not repeat), and as of 2026 several price cache hits below fresh input tokens; the layout rule is the same.
worked_examples: Reservation versus paging with 16 GB of case-study cache (147,456 B per token): reserving 8,192 tokens per request costs 1.21 GB, so 13 requests fit; if requests average 1,500 tokens, 18.3% of the reservation holds tokens. Paged with 16-token blocks, a 1,500-token request holds about 1,508 tokens (0.222 GB) on average, so about 72 fit at that moment, 5.5 times as many. Caveat: sequences grow, so the scheduler keeps headroom and preempts; the vLLM paper reports 2-4 times the throughput of earlier systems at the same latency.
Block arithmetic: a 37-token sequence with 16-token blocks uses 3 physical blocks with 11 unused slots; the worst-case waste per sequence is 15 tokens = 2.2 MB for the case study.

Prefix caching in the case study: each request is a 3,000-token stable prefix (system prompt, output schema and fixed reference text) + 1,000 tokens of hazard-log entries and request + 2,000 output tokens. Cold prefill: 7.61×10¹³ FLOPs (0.92 s on the 24 GB card); warm: 1.99×10¹³ (0.24 s), 3.8 times less, not 4, because the 1,000 new tokens still attend to all earlier positions. Memory: the shared 3,000 tokens (0.44 GB) are stored once, so each request holds 3,000 private tokens (0.44 GB) instead of 6,000 (0.885 GB), and 35 requests fit in 16 GB instead of 18.

Lab 2's prefix caching by hand on SmolLM2-135M (CPU, fp32): a 2,992-token system prompt; cold prefill about 8 s per request, warm about 0.16-0.30 s, last-position logits equal to within 4-7×10⁻⁵ (prototype values; writers use the lab's output).

Why does a 1,000-token warm prefill after a 3,000-token cached prefix cost more than a quarter of the 4,000-token cold prefill? -> The matmul FLOPs are a quarter, but each new token's attention still covers all earlier positions, including the cached 3,000.

sections.title: Number formats and the arithmetic of quantisation
sections.purpose: Give the formats and the exact arithmetic of mapping weights to a few bits, with the storage cost of the scales, so that every scheme in s8 is a variation on one formula.
must_cover: Why fewer bits: decode time is bytes per step over bandwidth (s1-s2), so every bit saved per weight speeds decode and frees memory for the cache (s3).

Float formats as (sign/exponent/mantissa bits; largest normal value; machine epsilon 2^-mantissa): fp32 1/8/23, 3.4×10³⁸, 1.2×10⁻⁷; fp16 1/5/10, 65,504, 9.8×10⁻⁴; bf16 1/8/7, 3.4×10³⁸, 7.8×10⁻³; fp8 E4M3 1/4/3, 448, 0.125; fp8 E5M2 1/5/2, 57,344, 0.25. Integers: int8 −128...127; int4 −8...7 (symmetric schemes use −7...7). Recap Module 08's training view in two sentences, then the inference view: fp16 can overflow on a model trained in bf16 whose activations exceed 65,504.

Block-scaled formats, dated and conservative: the OCP microscaling (MX) formats share one 8-bit power-of-two scale among 32 elements (MXFP4 elements are E2M1, giving 4 + 8/32 = 4.25 bits per value); 4-bit floating formats with block scales gained hardware support in datacentre GPUs from 2024-2025.

Symmetric (absmax) quantisation: s = max|w| / q_max with q_max = 2^(b−1) − 1; q = clip(round(w/s), −q_max, q_max); ŵ = s·q. Unclipped error |w − ŵ| ≤ s/2; if rounding errors are uniform on [−s/2, s/2] the mean squared error is s²/12 (derive the variance of the uniform distribution).
Asymmetric (zero-point, min-max) quantisation: s = (max w − min w)/(2^b − 1); z = round(−min w / s); q = clip(round(w/s) + z, 0, 2^b − 1); ŵ = s(q − z). It uses all levels when the values are skewed.

Granularity: per-tensor (one scale), per-channel (one scale per output row), group-wise (one scale per g consecutive weights along the input dimension, g = 32, 64 or 128). Storage: bits per weight = b + (bits of scale + bits of zero-point)/g.

Runtime: a per-output-channel scale factors out of the dot product, y_i = s_i Σ_j q_ij x_j, and is applied once per output; group scales must be applied per group inside the inner loop; weight-only kernels dequantise to fp16 in registers and multiply in fp16, so they save bytes, not FLOPs.
Round-to-nearest (RTN) is the baseline that every method in s8 improves on by choosing scales or roundings with data.
worked_examples: Zero-point int4 on the same vector: s = (0.91 + 0.48)/15 = 0.0927, z = round(0.48/0.0927) = 5; q = (6, 0, 5, 15, 4, 8, 1, 6); ŵ = (0.093, −0.463, 0, 0.927, −0.093, 0.278, −0.371, 0.093); RMS error 0.030, smaller because absmax never uses the levels −7, −6 and −5 when the most negative value is −0.48.

One outlier: replace 0.91 by 9.1. Absmax gives s = 1.3 and all seven ordinary weights round to 0: RMS error on them 0.246, against 0.042 before. With groups of 4, the outlier's group still zeroes its three companions, but the second group gets its own scale 0.33/7 = 0.047 and is quantised finely (ŵ = −0.047, 0.236, −0.33, 0.047): RMS error on the ordinary weights 0.188. The outlier spoils only its own group.

Bits per weight: int4 per-channel with an fp16 scale and 4,096 inputs: 4 + 16/4,096 = 4.004; group 128 with an fp16 scale only: 4.125 (the case study's scheme, s11); group 128 with fp16 scale and fp16 zero-point: 4.25; group 64 with scale only: 4.25; group 32 with scale only: 4.5. The case study's 8.305×10⁹ block weights at 4.25 bits: 4.41 GB (at 4.125 bits: 4.28 GB).

Why does a per-output-channel scale cost almost nothing at runtime while a group scale costs more? -> The channel scale multiplies the finished dot product once; group scales must be applied to partial sums inside the dot product.

sections.title: Quantising LLMs: outliers, GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant and the cache
sections.purpose: Explain why quantising a language model is harder than quantising a random matrix, what the calibrated methods do about it, how to quantise the cache, and how to measure the damage.
must_cover: What round-to-nearest does to a small model (Lab 4: SmolLM2-135M, perplexity on the first 4,096 tokens of the WikiText-2 test split; prototype values that writers replace with the lab's actual output): fp32 20.85; int8 per-tensor 21.57; int8 per-channel 21.04; int4 per-tensor about 5.8 million; int4 per-channel 48.4; int4 group-64 29.5; int4 group-64 with zero-point 27.4.

Outliers: weights are well behaved (in SmolLM2-135M the worst per-input-channel max/median ratio is about 12) but activations are not (in Lab 4 one input channel of layer 11's down-projection reaches 1,962 times the median channel). LLM.int8() (Dettmers et al. 2022) found large-magnitude features concentrated in a few hidden dimensions, emerging sharply in models of about 6.7B parameters and above, which break per-tensor int8 activation quantisation; its remedy is a mixed-precision decomposition: outlier dimensions in fp16, the rest in int8 with vector-wise scales, at a cost in kernel speed.

Weight-only (W4A16, W8A16) versus weight-and-activation (W8A8 in int8 or fp8), argued from the roofline: weight-only cuts the bytes of bandwidth-bound decode; prefill and large-batch decode are compute-bound and gain only from lower-precision arithmetic (int8 and fp8 tensor cores run at about twice the bf16 rate), which requires quantising the activations too.

SmoothQuant (Xiao et al. 2023): Y = XW = (X diag(s)⁻¹)(diag(s) W); choose per input channel j s_j = max|X_j|^α / max|W_j|^(1−α); α = 0.5 equalises the two maxima at √(max|X_j| · max|W_j|); the 1/s is folded into the preceding normalisation's weights, so it costs nothing at runtime. Show the identity and the equalisation.

GPTQ (Frantar et al. 2023): per layer, minimise ‖WX − ŴX‖²_F over quantised Ŵ, each row independently; with H = 2XX^T, quantise one column at a time and update the not-yet-quantised columns F to compensate: δ_F = −(w_q − Q(w_q)) / [H_F⁻¹]_qq · (H_F⁻¹)_{:,q} (the Optimal Brain Surgeon update; derive it with a Lagrange multiplier as an optional boxed derivation). GPTQ's engineering: one column order for all rows (a single inverse Hessian), lazy updates in blocks of 128 columns, a Cholesky form with dampening of 1% of the mean diagonal; calibration on 128 random 2,048-token segments of web text (C4); 175B-parameter models quantised in about four GPU hours.

AWQ (Lin et al. 2024): about 1% of weight channels are salient, and saliency follows activation magnitude, not weight magnitude; keeping them in fp16 recovers most of the loss, but mixed precision is awkward for kernels. Instead scale each salient input channel by s > 1 before quantisation and divide its activation by s: the channel's relative rounding error shrinks by about 1/s while the group's scale barely changes; search s = s_X^α over a small grid of α in [0, 1] to minimise the layer's output error on calibration data; no back-propagation or reconstruction, which makes it less prone to overfitting the calibration set; group size 128.

Cache quantisation: an 8-bit cache halves cache memory and cache reads (the case study: 18 → 36 sequences on the 24 GB card, at the same step time, so twice the aggregate throughput); keys have outlier channels, so per-channel scales for keys and per-token scales for values work better (KIVI, Liu et al. 2024, down to 2 bits); test at the longest contexts you serve.

Size matters (the source's rules, attributed): 8-bit weight-only is essentially free; 4-bit with GPTQ or AWQ cost under a point on most evaluations for models of 7B and above in those papers' experiments; below about 3B parameters 4 bits degrade noticeably. Lab 4's 135M model loses about 40% in perplexity at group-wise int4 RTN.

Measuring the damage: perplexity on WikiText-2 is the papers' convention (cheap and sensitive, but an average over generic text); then the deployed task's own evaluation (Module 09's suite; for the case study, parse rate and checker pass rate on held-out safety-case arguments); calibration data drawn from the deployment domain; evaluate the exact file that will be served and record its hash.

Formats in practice: GPTQ and AWQ checkpoints (int4 weights with group scales) for GPU engines; GGUF files with mixed 'k-quant' types for llama.cpp; NF4 (Module 09) is a storage format for QLoRA fine-tuning and less common for serving.
worked_examples: Precision choices for the case study on the 24 GB card (2.5 GB runtime overhead, 6,000-token sequences; the decode bound is for one sequence at a mean context of 5,000 tokens, weights plus 0.74 GB of cache, as everywhere in the module): bf16 19.1 GB → 2.4 GB of cache → 2 sequences, 50 tokens/s; int8 9.55 GB → 11.95 GB → 13 sequences, 97 tokens/s; 4-bit file 5.5 GB → 16 GB → 18 sequences, 160 tokens/s.

SmoothQuant on one channel with max|X_j| = 40 and max|W_j| = 0.5: α = 0.5 gives s = √80 = 8.94 and both maxima become 4.47; α = 0.75 gives s = 18.9, an activation maximum of 2.11 and a weight maximum of 9.46.
Lab 4 (prototype values): simulated W8A8 with per-tensor dynamic activation scales gives perplexity 40.7 (against 21.0 for int8 weights alone); with SmoothQuant α = 0.5, 26.4; with α = 0.8, 24.6.

SmoothQuant moves difficulty from activations to weights. Why is that a good trade? -> Weights are static and per-channel quantisation handles their mild outliers; activation outliers change from token to token and wreck per-tensor activation scales.

sections.title: Speeding up decode: speculative decoding and its relatives
sections.purpose: Derive speculative decoding: why verifying several tokens costs about one step, why the output distribution is exactly the large model's, and how much faster it is.
must_cover: The opportunity: a bandwidth-bound target model scores γ + 1 positions in about the time of one (s2), so a cheap draft model proposes γ tokens and the target checks them in one forward pass.

The algorithm (Leviathan, Kalman and Matias 2023; Chen et al. 2023): the draft samples x_1...x_γ autoregressively from q_1...q_γ; the target computes p_1...p_{γ+1} in one pass; for i = 1...γ accept x_i with probability min(1, p_i(x_i)/q_i(x_i)); at the first rejection sample a replacement from the residual r_i(x) = max(0, p_i(x) − q_i(x)) / Σ_y max(0, p_i(y) − q_i(y)) and stop; if all γ are accepted, sample a bonus token from p_{γ+1}. Each iteration emits between 1 and γ + 1 tokens.

Proof that the output is distributed as p (write it out): P(output = x) = q(x)·min(1, p(x)/q(x)) + (1 − β)·r(x), where β = Σ_x min(p(x), q(x)) is the probability of acceptance; the first term equals min(p(x), q(x)); Σ_y max(0, p(y) − q(y)) = 1 − β, so the second term equals p(x) − min(p(x), q(x)); the sum is p(x). Hence the acceptance rate α = E[β] = 1 − TV(p, q), one minus the total-variation distance between target and draft.

Greedy special case: accept x_i if and only if it equals the target's argmax; the output equals the target's own greedy output, except where verifying several positions at once changes the logits in the last bits at a near-tie (Lab 5 checks this).
Expected tokens per iteration: with acceptances independent with probability α, P(at least k drafts accepted) = α^k for k ≤ γ, so E[tokens] = 1 + Σ_{k=1}^{γ} α^k = (1 − α^{γ+1})/(1 − α).

Walltime: an iteration costs γ draft steps and one verification, (γc + v)·T_target, where c is the draft-to-target step-cost ratio and v ≈ 1 when verification is bandwidth-bound; speed-up S = (1 − α^{γ+1}) / ((1 − α)(γc + v)). This corrects the source's shorthand 'the speed-up is the acceptance rate': it depends on α, γ and c together.

When it fails: a low acceptance rate (a draft from another family or domain, a fine-tuned target with an untuned draft, high temperature); an expensive draft (c large); high load (at large batch the GPU approaches compute-bound, verifying B(γ + 1) tokens is no longer free, and the gain shrinks or turns negative); different tokenizers (draft and target must share a vocabulary).

Relatives: Medusa (Cai et al. 2024) adds decoding heads to the target that propose several future tokens, verified together with tree attention; EAGLE (Li et al. 2024) drafts with a light head that autoregresses on the target's top-layer features; prompt-lookup decoding (Saxena 2023) drafts by copying the continuation of a matching n-gram from the context, at almost no cost and with high acceptance when the output copies the input (editing, extraction, checking an existing safety argument); lookahead decoding (Fu et al. 2024) generates n-grams in parallel by Jacobi iteration.

Other routes to faster decode, from the source: distillation into a smaller model trades quality for speed permanently (Module 09); mixture-of-experts models read only the active experts per token but must hold all of them in memory, and at large batch different tokens route to different experts, so the bytes per step rise toward the total.
worked_examples: Speed-ups with v = 1: α = 0.8, γ = 4, c = 0.05: E = 3.36 tokens per iteration, S = 3.36/1.2 = 2.80; α = 0.6 with the same γ and c: E = 2.31, S = 1.92; α = 0.8, γ = 4, c = 0.4 (about the CPU lab's ratio): S = 1.29. For α = 0.8, c = 0.05, S(γ = 1...8) = 1.71, 2.22, 2.57, 2.80, 2.95, 3.04, 3.08, 3.09: diminishing returns. For α = 0.7, c = 0.4 the best γ is 2 (S = 1.22), and γ ≥ 5 is slower than not speculating (0.98 at γ = 5).

Lab 5 on a CPU (prototype values): SmolLM2-135M drafting for SmolLM2-360M, greedy, 5 prompts × 64 new tokens: α̂ = 0.871, 0.865 and 0.874 at γ = 2, 4 and 6 (each γ's run gives its own estimate); at γ = 4, 3.86 tokens per iteration against 3.82 predicted from that run's α̂; outputs identical to the target's greedy outputs on every prompt. Measured c ≈ 0.49, and a 5-token verification cost about 1.6 target steps, so the formula E/(γc + v) predicts 3.82/(4 × 0.49 + 1.6) = 1.07× at γ = 4; the measured speed-up, 1.22×, is 14% above the prediction, a reminder that step costs timed in isolation on a busy CPU are only a rough guide (the lab prints both). On a GPU with a draft 30-100 times smaller than the target, c falls to a few hundredths and the formula with the same α gives about 3× (γ = 4, c = 0.05, v = 1: 3.86/1.2 = 3.2), close to the two to three times reported on text where the draft is good.

Mixture of experts at decode: a model shaped like Mixtral 8x7B (46.7B parameters in total, 12.9B active per token) at 4.9 bits per weight is a 28.6 GB file, too large for a 24 GB card, while one token reads only 7.9 GB, about 127 tokens/s on a 1 TB/s card if it fitted.

Why is the output distribution unchanged even with a poor draft? -> The acceptance test and the residual resampling exactly restore the probability mass the draft got wrong; a poor draft only lowers α and therefore the speed-up.

sections.title: Structured output and the serving engine
sections.purpose: Show how a server can guarantee that output follows a schema, and what a serving engine is made of, so that the reader can choose and configure one.
must_cover: Constrained decoding (Module 07 introduced it as masking invalid tokens; recall that in a sentence and link, then show how a serving engine builds the mask): compile a JSON schema or regular expression into a finite-state machine over characters (a context-free grammar for nested structures, into a pushdown automaton); for each automaton state, precompute the set of vocabulary tokens that keep the output a valid prefix (Willard and Louf 2023, the token-level index behind the Outlines library); at each step set the logits of all other tokens to −∞, renormalise, sample, and advance the state.

What it guarantees and what it does not: syntax, not content. When the model's preferred continuation is invalid, the mask forces the most probable valid one, so content must still be checked; token boundaries can make a grammar awkward for a model; schemas the model was trained on (Module 09's tool-call formats) fit best; run structured output at temperature 0 or low; mask computation must be fast enough not to stall the GPU (engines precompile grammars).

Engine anatomy: API server (OpenAI-compatible, streaming); tokenizer and chat template; scheduler (waiting and running queues, admission, preemption, chunked prefill); KV block manager (paging, prefix cache); model runner (fused attention kernels such as FlashAttention and paged attention, quantised matrix kernels, captured CUDA graphs); sampler (temperature, top-p, grammar masks, speculative verification); detokeniser and streamer; metrics endpoint.

The stacks, as of 2026 (check current documentation): vLLM: the general-purpose GPU server with PagedAttention, continuous batching, prefix caching, many quantised formats, speculative decoding, multi-LoRA serving and an OpenAI-compatible API; SGLang: similar, with RadixAttention prefix sharing and strong structured-output and multi-call scheduling; TensorRT-LLM: NVIDIA's compiled path, the fastest on its hardware and the most setup; Hugging Face Text Generation Inference (TGI): widely deployed from 2023 (check its current maintenance status before adopting it); llama.cpp and Ollama: CPUs, Apple silicon and consumer GPUs with GGUF quantised files, single-machine use.

The OpenAI-compatible chat-completions API: POST /v1/chat/completions with model, messages (role, content), max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop, stream, and response_format or tools; streamed responses arrive as server-sent events ('data: {json}' lines ending with 'data: [DONE]'); the usage field gives prompt and completion tokens; finish_reason 'length' means max_tokens cut the output. A client written for a hosted API is pointed at a local server by changing its base URL, API key and model name.

The chat template: the server renders messages into tokens with the template stored with the model's tokenizer; it must be identical to the one used in post-training (Module 09). Test it by rendering one conversation through the server and through the training pipeline and comparing the tokens.
Several fine-tuned adapters on one base (Module 09): engines can apply LoRA adapters per request over one copy of the base weights; each adapter has its own prefix cache.
Cross-link the AI Agents series for building clients, tool calling and structured outputs at the application level.
worked_examples: A constrained field: the schema allows 'severity' to be one of S1, S2, S3, S4 (a hazard log's severity categories). At the position after '"severity": "' a toy vocabulary {S, S1, S3, High, ", }} has logits (1.0, 2.0, 0.5, 3.0, 0.2, −1.0); unconstrained probabilities (0.081, 0.221, 0.049, 0.601, 0.037, 0.011): the model prefers 'High' at 60%. The mask allows S, S1 and S3; renormalised: (0.231, 0.629, 0.140). The output is valid, but the model's preferred content was not representable: the schema or the prompt is wrong, which a content check, not the parser, will reveal.

Pointing a client at a local server: base URL http://localhost:8000/v1 (vLLM's default port), http://localhost:8080/v1 (llama-server's) or http://localhost:11434/v1 (Ollama's) instead of the hosted endpoint; the served model's name; any non-empty API key if the server does not check one; the request body unchanged.

Serving-engine block diagram: client → API server (OpenAI-compatible, server-sent-event streaming) → tokenizer and chat template → scheduler (waiting queue, running batch, preemption) ↔ KV block manager (block tables, prefix cache, free list) → model runner on the GPU (attention and quantised GEMM kernels) → sampler (temperature and top-p, grammar mask, speculative verification) → detokeniser → stream back to the client; a metrics endpoint tapping the scheduler and the block manager.

checks: A client moves from a hosted API to a self-hosted vLLM server. Which settings change, and which must be re-checked? -> The base URL, API key and model name change; re-check the chat template the server applies, its default sampling parameters (temperature) and the maximum context.
Does grammar-constrained decoding guarantee a correct safety argument? -> No: it guarantees the syntax; the content can still be wrong, and the mask can force a valid but unintended value.

sections.title: Sizing the running case study
sections.purpose: Put s1-s10 together to size the serving of the hypothetical 9.5B safety-case model on one 24 GB GPU and on larger cards, ending with cost per million tokens and what the real utilisation does to it.
must_cover: The case (hypothetical, as in Modules 07-09): the open-weight bilingual (English-Chinese) model of about 9.5B parameters chosen in Module 07 and adapted in Modules 08-09 to draft and check safety-case arguments for the pressure-relief system of a reactor vessel; Module 09 merges its LoRA adapter into bf16 weights, and this module quantises and serves that artifact. Configuration (Module 07's): L = 36, d = 4,096, 32 query heads, 8 KV heads, d_head = 128, d_ff = 15,360 (SwiGLU), vocabulary 152,064, untied embeddings: N = 9.55×10⁹ parameters, of which N_matmul = 8.93×10⁹ take part in matrix multiplications (all but the input embedding). Requests (the series workload, Module 07): 4,000 tokens in (a 3,000-token stable prefix of system prompt, output schema and fixed reference text, plus 1,000 tokens of hazard-log entries and the engineer's request) and 2,000 out (for example a 20-entry hazard log for the pressure-relief system, or an argument fragment with evidence references), at 2,000 requests a day.

Step 1, weights: recall the count, attention 41,943,040 + feed-forward 188,743,680 + norms 8,192 = 230,694,912 parameters per layer (230.7M), × 36 = 8.305×10⁹, plus 2 × 0.623×10⁹ for the embedding and output head. The file is then 8.305×10⁹ × 4.125/8 = 4.28 GB for the blocks (symmetric int4 with one fp16 scale per 128 weights, s7) plus 1.25 GB for the embedding and head kept at 8 bits = 5.53 GB, written 5.5 GB. In bf16 the same model is 19.1 GB.
Step 2, memory budget: 24 − 5.5 − 2.5 = 16 GB for the cache, where 2.5 GB for the runtime (context, activation workspace, graph buffers) is an assumption to measure on your own stack.
Step 3, concurrency: 6,000 × 147,456 B = 0.885 GB per finished request → 18 concurrent; an 8-bit cache → 36; sharing the 3,000-token stable prefix (s6) → 35 with a bf16 cache.

Step 4, latency at low load: TTFT = 7.61×10¹³ / (0.5 × 165×10¹²) = 0.92 s (0.24 s when the prefix is cached); TPOT = (5.5 + 0.74) GB / 1.0 TB/s = 6.24 ms at the mean context of 5,000 tokens; 2,000 tokens in 12.5 s; about 13.4 s end to end.

Step 5, throughput at full load: B = 18 gives an 18.8 ms step and 959 tokens/s while decoding; but prefills share the GPU. GPU time per request = 0.92 s of prefill + 2,000 × 18.8 ms / 18 = 2.09 s of decode = 3.0 s, so about 1,200 requests per hour, 2.4 million output tokens per hour (665 tokens/s averaged). Each request then takes about 55 s end to end, because prefills take 31% of the GPU's time and stretch the effective TPOT to about 27 ms. Little's law check (s12): 0.33 requests/s × 55 s ≈ 18 requests in the system, the cache's limit.

Step 6, other cards (same model, same requests): 24 GB at 0.30 TB/s (L4 class): 18 sequences, 48 tokens/s single-stream, 288 tokens/s at full batch; 48 GB at 0.864 TB/s (L40S class): 40 GB of cache, 45 sequences, 139 / 1,005; 80 GB at 2.04 TB/s (A100): 72 GB, 81 sequences, 327 / 2,532; 80 GB at 3.35 TB/s (H100 SXM): 81 sequences, 537 / 4,161.

Step 7, cost, with every price an assumption, as of 2026, written in USD: cost per million output tokens = price per GPU-hour / (output tokens per hour / 10⁶). Module 07 priced tokens from FLOPs; here they are priced from a GPU-hour and a throughput. At an assumed USD 1.00 per GPU-hour for the 24 GB card (invite the reader to substitute a current quote): USD 1.00 / 2.40 = USD 0.42 per million output tokens at full utilisation; USD 1.39 at 30%. Utilisation decides it: the case study's 2,000 requests a day need 2,000 × 3.0 s = 1.67 GPU-hours, 6.9% of one card, so an always-on card costs USD 24 a day, USD 0.012 per request or USD 6.00 per million output tokens, against USD 0.42 at full utilisation. The same traffic through a hosted API at Module 07's assumed prices (USD 0.20 and 0.80 per million input and output tokens, cached input at 10% of the input price) costs USD 4.80 a day, or USD 3.72 with the 3,000-token prefix cached; the card breaks even near 10,000 requests a day (about 13,000 against the cached API), within its capacity under the SLO (step 8) if the traffic is spread over the day. At the case study's volume, then, the reasons to self-host are not cost (Module 07): data that may not leave the site, control of the model version, and serving the fine-tuned model itself. For an owned card: amortised purchase plus power, for example an assumed USD 2,000 over three years of continuous use (USD 0.076/h) plus 0.45 kW at an assumed USD 0.20/kWh (USD 0.09/h). Energy: 450 W / 665 tokens/s ≈ 0.68 J per output token. Compare with a hosted model only at equal quality on your task and at your real utilisation, and meter the actual figure (s13).

Step 8, the SLO changes the answer: with p99 TTFT ≤ 3 s and p99 inter-token latency ≤ 100 ms, Lab 3's simulator sustains about 0.22 requests/s (about 790 an hour) on the 24 GB card and prints about 423 output tokens/s at that rate, about 70% of its saturation throughput (590 tokens/s); at the assumed USD 1.00/h that is USD 1.00 / 1.52 = USD 0.66 per million output tokens. Take the cost from the printed throughput: Lab 3's output lengths are lognormal (median 1,500, mean about 1,740 after the clip at max_tokens = 4,000), while this section sizes for 2,000.

What the estimate leaves out: tokenizer and scheduler CPU time, preemption at the tail, kernels running below the bounds, the occasional request that needs 32,000 tokens of cache; validate with a load test (s12; Labs 3 and 6).

sections.title: Measuring latency: metrics, load tests and SLOs
sections.purpose: Define the latency metrics of LLM serving, show how load turns into queueing, and explain how to run a load test whose numbers can be trusted.
must_cover: Metrics: TTFT (request sent to first token received: queueing + prefill + network); TPOT = (E2E − TTFT)/(n_out − 1); inter-token latency (ITL), every gap between streamed tokens, whose tail shows the prefill stalls that TPOT averages away; end-to-end latency; throughput in output tokens/s and requests/s; goodput, the rate of requests that meet every SLO (the term used by DistServe).
Percentiles: report p50, p90 and p99 computed from raw samples; never average percentiles across servers or time windows; the mean hides the tail.

Tail amplification (Dean and Barroso 2013): an agent that makes 20 sequential calls, each slower than its p99 with probability 1%, has 1 − 0.99²⁰ = 18.2% of its tasks hit at least one slow call; with 50 calls, 39.5%.

Queueing: utilisation ρ = arrival rate / service rate; in an M/M/1 queue the mean time in the system is S/(1 − ρ), with S the mean service time: 2S at ρ = 0.5, 5S at 0.8, 10S at 0.9, 20S at 0.95. An LLM server is not M/M/1 (batching raises its service rate with load), but the knee is real: in Lab 3 the median TTFT of continuous batching rises from about 1.2 s at 0.25 requests/s to about 13 s at 0.30.
Little's law L = λW holds for any stable system: the mean number of requests in the system equals the arrival rate times the mean time in the system. Use it to check a load test and a sizing (s11).

Load-test design: open-loop arrivals (Poisson at a set rate) expose overload; closed-loop tests (N users, each waiting for its reply) slow their own arrivals when the server slows and hide the overload (coordinated omission). Use production length distributions; stream and timestamp tokens at the client; warm up; sweep the rate past the knee; report hardware, engine version, model hash, quantisation, prompt and output lengths and the arrival rate with every number.

SLOs: write them per use. For the case study, an interactive drafting assistant: p99 TTFT ≤ 3 s and p99 ITL ≤ 100 ms (streaming at 10 tokens/s or faster keeps ahead of a reader); overnight batch checking: throughput and a completion deadline only. Capacity is the highest arrival rate at which the SLO holds (goodput), not the saturation throughput.
Benchmarks that mislead: tokens/s that include prompt tokens; one request on an idle server; closed-loop concurrency without arrival rates; unstated lengths.
worked_examples: Tail amplification: 1 − 0.99²⁰ = 0.182 and 1 − 0.99⁵⁰ = 0.395.
M/M/1 time in system relative to the service time: ρ = 0.5: 2; 0.8: 5; 0.9: 10; 0.95: 20.

Lab 3's sweep for the case study on the 24 GB card (prototype values; writers use the lab's output): at 0.20 requests/s, continuous batching with on-demand cache allocation and a 256-token prefill budget per iteration gives p50/p99 TTFT of 1.1/2.9 s and p99 ITL of 62 ms; at 0.25 requests/s p99 TTFT is 7.4 s; at 0.30, 22 s. Without chunking the worst gap is about 2.3 s (several prompts prefilled in one iteration); with it, 66 ms.

Your p50 TTFT is 0.4 s but p99 is 9 s, while TPOT is fine. What is the most likely cause? -> Requests queueing behind long prefills at a utilisation near the knee; chunked prefill, admission control or more capacity.

sections.title: Reliability in production
sections.purpose: List what keeps a self-hosted model trustworthy in service: knowing exactly what is running, failing over cleanly, measuring cost, being honest about determinism, and protecting what users send.
must_cover: Versioning and provenance: the served artifact is the exact quantised weights file plus the tokenizer, the chat template, the engine version, the sampling defaults and the system prompt; hash each (SHA-256); a deployment is a change of hash; record the hashes and the sampling parameters with every output, so that any output can be traced to what produced it. This is the same discipline as versioning any numerical tool whose outputs others rely on, such as a solver or a compiler.
Rollout: shadow or canary a new hash with the evaluation suite (Module 09) and live metrics; rollback is redeploying the previous hash.

Health and capacity: liveness (the process answers) versus readiness (the model is loaded and has capacity); a health endpoint reporting the loaded model's hash, cache utilisation and queue depth; alerts on queue depth, p99 TTFT, error rate and preemption rate.

Timeouts, retries and fallback: a time budget per request; retry with exponential backoff and jitter only when nothing has yet been streamed to the user (a retry after partial output produces a different answer); a circuit breaker stops traffic to a failing server; fall back to a second server or a hosted model, record which model produced each output, and exercise the fallback on a schedule (a failover drill, or a small share of live traffic), because an unexercised fallback fails when it is needed.
Metering: tokens in and out per request, per application and per customer or team, in a usage ledger, so cost is measured rather than assumed (s11).

Determinism: temperature 0 makes the sampling rule deterministic, not the arithmetic. Floating-point addition is not associative; kernels choose reduction orders by batch shape, so the same request computes slightly different logits depending on what else is in the batch; where two candidates are nearly tied the argmax flips and the rest of the output diverges. Other sources: a prefix-cache hit versus a miss, speculative verification, different GPUs, drivers or engine versions. Batch-invariant kernels can remove this at a throughput cost (as of 2025-2026). Test reproducibility claims (Lab 6 tests it on a CPU); accept outputs because they pass their checks (schema validation, the domain's rule checks, human review), not because they are byte-identical to an earlier run.

Privacy: prompts are user data. Log hashes, sizes and timings by default; log content only under a written retention policy with access control. A prefix cache shared between tenants can reveal through timing that another tenant sent the same prefix; isolate caches per tenant where that matters. Prompt injection and guardrails belong to the AI Agents series.
worked_examples: A provenance record for one case-study output: weights SHA-256; tokenizer and template hashes; engine name and version; quantisation scheme (int4 blocks with one fp16 scale per 128 weights, 8-bit embedding and head); sampling (temperature 0, max_tokens 2,000); system-prompt version; request id; token counts (4,012 in, 1,876 out); TTFT and E2E; fallback flag.

Determinism under batching (the source's Exercise 3, done in Lab 6): run one prompt greedily alone and as one left-padded row of a batch of 8; compare the tokens, the largest logit difference and the smallest top-2 logit gap. On the preparation CPU in float32: identical tokens, logits differing by at most 4.8×10⁻⁵, and a smallest gap of 0.056 over 64 tokens, about a thousand times larger, so nothing flipped; a flip needs a near-tie inside the noise, which lower precision, longer outputs and more traffic make likely.

checks: Why should a retry not be automatic after the first tokens have been streamed? -> The user has already seen part of an answer; the retry may produce a different one, and the duplicate costs tokens. Return the error and let the client decide.

After a deployment the weights file has the same SHA-256 as before, yet outputs at temperature 0 changed across the evaluation suite. Name three things that may have changed, and how the provenance record shows which. -> The tokenizer, the chat template, the engine version (and with it the kernels), the sampling defaults or the system prompt; each has its own hash or version in the record, so comparing the records of an old and a new output names the change.
