what_goes_wrong: The server preempts constantly or rejects requests when one long document arrives -> the cache was sized for the average request (6,000 tokens, 0.885 GB) while a 32,000-token request needs 4.7 GB, five average requests' worth -> size for the longest request you accept, set the maximum model length explicitly, keep headroom, and give long requests their own queue or server.

The model ignores the system prompt in production but follows it in evaluation -> the server's chat template differs from the one used in post-training -> serve the template shipped with the fine-tuned tokenizer; before every deployment render one conversation through the server and through the training pipeline and compare the tokens.

A check that passed at bf16 fails after deployment -> the 4-bit weights were promoted without re-evaluation -> evaluate the exact quantised file with the full suite, record its hash, and deploy only that hash.

The prefix-cache hit rate is zero -> the system prompt changes on every request (a timestamp, a request id or a user name at the top) -> put stable content first and variable content last, and monitor the hit rate.

Structured outputs vary between runs or are malformed -> the temperature was left at the server default (often 1.0) and no grammar was enforced -> set temperature 0 or low, enable constrained decoding, and validate content as well as syntax.
The fallback fails on the day the GPU does -> it was never exercised -> route a small share of live traffic through it continuously, or run a failover drill on a schedule.

Quality degrades slowly, worst on long inputs, with no errors anywhere -> positions are miscounted after prefix caching or between prefill and decode, so the RoPE angles are wrong -> compare cached with uncached logits to a tolerance on long prompts (Lab 2) after every engine or model change.

Throughput is far below the roofline estimate -> the batch is held small (a low limit on running sequences or a small cache fraction), tokenisation or sampling is CPU-bound, or the kernels do not support the quantised format and fall back to slow paths -> measure MBU and GPU utilisation, raise the batch limits, profile the host side, confirm the quantised kernels are in use.

p99 TTFT spikes while p50 is fine -> long prompts' prefills stall the batch and requests queue at a utilisation near the knee -> chunked prefill, admission control, a separate queue for long prompts, or more capacity.

Turning on speculative decoding makes serving slower -> the acceptance rate is low (a mismatched or untuned draft, high temperature) or the load is high, so verification is no longer free -> measure the acceptance rate per workload, and disable speculation above a load threshold.

A reproducibility claim fails an audit: two runs at temperature 0 differ -> batch-composition-dependent numerics flip near-tied tokens -> do not promise byte equality; record provenance, accept outputs by their checks, and use batch-invariant kernels where reproducibility is a requirement.

Outputs end in the middle of a structure -> max_tokens is too small, or prompt + max_tokens exceeds the context window -> check finish_reason ('length'), budget tokens per request, and reject oversize inputs explicitly.

Perplexity barely moves after quantisation but task accuracy drops -> perplexity averages over generic text, while the task depends on rare tokens, long reasoning or exact copying -> evaluate the deployed task with domain calibration data before and after quantising.

A published serving benchmark cannot be reproduced -> it counted prompt tokens in tokens/s, measured one request on an idle server, or used closed-loop concurrency with unstated lengths -> report TTFT, ITL and output throughput separately, with lengths, arrival rate, hardware and versions.

labs.title: A roofline and sizing calculator
labs.goal: Turn the formulas of s1-s4 into a small calculator that sizes any model on any accelerator, reproduce the case study's sizing table, and measure the roofline of your own machine.
labs.data: None to download: model and accelerator figures are typed in from s3, s4 and s11; the machine measurement multiplies random float32 matrices.
steps: Define dataclasses Model(name, n_layers, d_model, n_heads, n_kv_heads, d_head, d_ff, vocab, tied, weight_bytes), with properties n_params (for memory) and n_matmul (for FLOPs: n_params less the input embedding when the embeddings are untied, Module 06's convention), and Accelerator(name, mem_gb, bw_tb_s, tflops). Create the case-study model (36 layers, d_model 4,096, 32 query heads, 8 KV heads, d_head 128, d_ff 15,360, vocabulary 152,064, untied) and print n_params = 9,550,729,216 and n_matmul = 8,927,875,072; print its 4-bit file size from the s11 breakdown, 8.305e9 × 4.125/8 + 1.246e9 × 1 byte = 5.53 GB, then set weight_bytes = 5.5e9 as the text does; add bf16 (19.10 GB) and int8 (9.55 GB) variants.
kv_bytes_per_token(model, b) = 2·L·n_kv·d_head·b. Print 147,456 B (bf16) and 73,728 B (8-bit), and 0.885 GB for one 6,000-token request.

prefill_s(model, acc, T, mfu=0.5) = (2·N_matmul·T + 2·L·d·T²)/(mfu·peak) and decode_step_s(model, acc, B, ctx, b_kv=2) = max((W + B·kv·ctx)/BW, (2·N_matmul·B + 4·L·d·B·ctx)/peak). Print 0.92 s for a 4,000-token prompt on the 24GB-1.0TB/s card and 6.24 ms for one sequence at 5,000 tokens of context.

size(model, acc, overhead_gb=2.5, prompt=4000, out=2000) prints the cache budget, the maximum number of concurrent 6,000-token requests, TTFT, single-stream tokens/s at mean context 5,000 and aggregate tokens/s at maximum concurrency. Expected rows: 24GB-1.0: 16.0 GB, 18, 0.92 s, 160, 959; 24GB-0.3: 16.0 GB, 18, 1.26 s, 48, 288; 48GB: 40.0 GB, 45, 0.42 s, 139, 1,005; 80GB-2.0: 72.0 GB, 81, 0.49 s, 327, 2,532; 80GB-3.35: 72.0 GB, 81, 0.15 s, 537, 4,161. Repeat for the bf16 and int8 variants on the 24GB-1.0 card: 2 and 13 concurrent requests, 50 and 97 tokens/s single-stream.

Plot a log-log roofline for the 24GB-1.0 and 80GB-3.35 cards with four points for a 4,096 × 4,096 bf16 matmul at B = 1, 16, 256 and 2,048 (intensity 1.0, 15.9, 227.6, 1,024); save roofline.png (fig-10-2).

Measure this machine: time W @ X for an 8,192 × 8,192 float32 W (268 MB, 256 MiB, larger than any CPU cache) and B in {1, 2, 4, ..., 512}, taking the median of 5 runs after a warm-up; print ms, GFLOP/s, GB/s and intensity; estimate bandwidth from B = 1 (the decode case) and peak from the largest B; add the points to the plot as 'this CPU' and print its ridge point. Preparation values (4 threads, a desktop shared with other jobs; they varied by up to 2× between runs): about 12.6 GB/s at B = 1, so about 21 ms for this matrix (15-17 ms in a later run); B = 2 took about 1.7 times as long as B = 1, because PyTorch hands a one-column product to a separate matrix-vector kernel, and from B = 2 to 16 the time barely changed; about 200-250 GFLOP/s at B = 512.

Predict this CPU's decode time per token for SmolLM2-135M (538 MB of float32 weights) and SmolLM2-360M (1,447 MB) from the measured bandwidth, and keep the numbers for Labs 5 and 6. On the preparation machine, at the 12.6 GB/s measured in the same session as Lab 5's step costs, the bounds are 42.7 and 114.9 ms against Lab 5's measured 57 and 116 ms: 1.3 times the bound for the 135M model and about equal to it for the 360M model, whose larger matrices hide the per-operation overheads that a 30-layer model of small matrices pays on a CPU.
expected_observations: The calculator reproduces s11's table; the two 24 GB cards hold the same 18 requests but differ 3.3-fold in decode speed.
On the roofline, batch-1 decode sits about 300 times below the H100's ridge; only prefill-sized products reach the flat roof.

On your CPU the matmul time barely changes between B = 2 and B ≈ 16 (B = 1 may be faster still, through a separate matrix-vector kernel): the weights are read once and the extra columns are almost free, which is why batching helps decode; past the CPU's ridge (about 15-20 FLOP/byte) the time grows in proportion to B.
Achieved CPU bandwidth is well below the memory's theoretical figure, a reminder that datasheet numbers are ceilings.
extensions: Add an Apple M2 Ultra profile (192 GB, 0.8 TB/s) and size a 70B-class model at 4 bits on it.
Model two 24 GB cards with tensor parallelism as one device of 48 GB, 2.0 TB/s and 330 TFLOP/s with an assumed 10% communication penalty, and compare it with one 48 GB card.
Plot aggregate and per-sequence tokens/s against B for each card (fig-10-7) and mark where each runs out of memory.

labs.title: A KV cache for a small decoder, and prefix caching by hand
labs.goal: Add a KV cache to a small decoder, prove it exact, measure what it saves and how big it is, see how position bugs hide, and reuse a cached prefix on a real model.
labs.data: Steps 1-7 use a randomly initialised decoder (no download). Step 8 downloads HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M (269 MB, reused in Labs 4, 5 and 6).
steps: Define a compact decoder with the modern block of Module 06: RMSNorm, RoPE, grouped-query attention with 8 query heads and 2 KV heads of d_head 32, SwiGLU with d_ff 688; d = 256, L = 4, vocabulary 512, maximum length 1,024; float32; random weights after torch.manual_seed(0). Print the parameter count, 3,033,344. A reader who kept the Module 06 model can make the same edits to it; correctness and timing do not depend on training.

generate_nocache(prompt, n): greedy decoding that runs the model on the whole sequence at every step and keeps the last position's logits. The prompt is 16 random token ids from torch.Generator().manual_seed(1).

Add the cache: each block keeps K and V tensors of shape (B, n_kv, T, d_head); the model's forward takes start_pos so that RoPE uses absolute positions; new keys and values are appended along T; the causal mask is aligned to the end (new query i sees keys up to T_cached + i). generate_cache(prompt, n) prefills the prompt, then feeds one token at a time.
Verify for n = 256: tokens identical (True) and the maximum absolute logit difference over all steps about 1.7×10⁻⁶ (float32 rounding).
Measure the cache: sum the bytes of every K and V tensor: 555,008 bytes for 271 cached tokens, exactly 2·L·n_kv·d_head·4 bytes·T = 2·4·2·32·4·271.

Time n = 64, 128, 256 and 512 with and without the cache and print seconds and ms per token. On the preparation machine: without the cache 0.38, 0.83, 3.2 and 11.4 s; with it 0.19, 0.27, 0.72 and 2.3 s.

Inject two position bugs and print tokens-identical and the maximum logit difference for each: (a) off by one (start_pos − 1 for decode tokens): tokens still identical over 256 steps, logits differ by up to about 0.03; (b) a frozen position (every decode token at position 16): the tokens diverge at about the 23rd generated token and the logits differ by about 3.6. Lesson: compare logits with a tolerance against the uncached reference; token equality is a weak test.

Prefix caching by hand on SmolLM2-135M (float32): build a system prompt of about 3,000 tokens by repeating a fixed 60-word paragraph about safety-case structure 40 times with numbered rules (2,992 tokens with the SmolLM2 tokenizer), and three short questions. Cold: run system prompt + question for each question; record the time and the last-position logits. Warm: run the system prompt once into a transformers DynamicCache; for each question, copy.deepcopy the cache and run only the question tokens with past_key_values. Print the times (preparation machine: cold about 8 s per request; the prefix once about 8 s; warm 0.16-0.30 s) and the maximum logit difference from the cold run (4-7×10⁻⁵).
expected_observations: With the cache, decoding is exact: identical tokens and logits equal to rounding error.

Without the cache the time per token grows with the sequence (the total grows roughly quadratically); with it, the time per token grows only slowly (attention over a longer cache, plus the concatenation copy).
The cache's measured bytes match 2·L·n_kv·d_head·b·T exactly.
A position that is off by one is invisible in the tokens and visible in the logits; a frozen position eventually changes the text.
Reusing a cached 3,000-token prefix makes each request's prefill 25-50 times faster on a CPU, with logits equal to within 10⁻⁴: the saving of s6.
extensions: Pre-allocate the cache (fixed tensors written by index) instead of torch.cat and compare the time per token at n = 1,024.
Change n_kv from 2 to 8 (multi-head) and to 1 (multi-query) and check that the cache bytes follow the formula.
Quantise the cached keys and values to int8 per token (absmax over d_head) and measure the logit error.
In step 8, change one character at the start of the system prompt and confirm that no part of the cached prefix can be reused.

labs.title: A continuous-batching simulator
labs.goal: Simulate static and continuous batching, cache-admission policies and chunked prefill for the case study on the 24 GB card, and find the knee of the latency-throughput curve and the capacity under an SLO.
labs.data: Synthetic: Poisson arrivals and random prompt and output lengths, seeded.
steps: Iteration cost model (from Lab 1): an iteration with decoding contexts c_i and prefill chunks of k_j new tokens after c_j cached tokens costs max(bytes/BW, FLOPs/(0.5·peak)), with FLOPs = 2·N_matmul(#decodes + Σk_j) + 4·L·d·(Σc_i + Σ(k_j·c_j + k_j(k_j + 1)/2)) and bytes = W + kv·(Σc_i + Σc_j); N_matmul = 8.93×10⁹, L = 36, d = 4,096, W = 5.5×10⁹, kv = 147,456, BW = 1.0×10¹², peak = 165×10¹². Print: a 4,000-token prefill alone 0.92 s; 18 decodes at a 5,000-token context 18.8 ms; with 17 decodes at a 5,000-token context, a 512-token chunk that opens its prompt (no cached prefix) 116 ms and one that follows 2,000 cached prompt tokens 123 ms; a 128-token chunk 32 and 34 ms (all compute-bound: the bytes alone take 18 ms).

Workload: Poisson arrivals at rate λ; prompt lengths uniform integers in [2,000, 6,000]; output lengths lognormal with median 1,500 and σ = 0.6, clipped to [16, 4,000] (max_tokens = 4,000; the clip lowers the mean from 1,800 to about 1,730, and the seeded sample's mean is 1,737); 300 requests; random.Random(0), drawing each request's arrival gap, prompt length and output length in that order, so the lengths are the same at every λ.

Static batching: batches of up to 16, dispatched when 16 are waiting or 2 s after the oldest waiting request arrived, whichever comes first, and only when the GPU is free; one prefill iteration for the whole batch, then decode iterations until the longest request finishes (finished slots stay in the batch as padding). Say that the simulator does not check memory for static batches: their cache reaches about 20 GB at 0.20 requests/s and above (worst case 16 × 10,000 tokens × 147,456 B = 23.6 GB), more than the 16 GB budget, so static batching is flattered and still loses.

Continuous batching with reserve-max admission: at every iteration admit waiting requests (first come first served, at most 256 running) while the reserved cache (prompt + 4,000 tokens per running request) fits in the 16 GB budget; admitted prompts are prefilled whole in that iteration alongside the decodes.

Continuous batching with on-demand (paged) admission: admit while the cache actually in use plus the new prompt fits within 99% of the budget; when a step would overflow, preempt the most recently admitted request (free its cache, put it at the front of the queue; on readmission it re-prefills its prompt and the tokens generated so far). Count preemptions.
Chunked prefill: as the on-demand policy, but at most 256 prompt tokens per iteration, shared among the requests still prefilling.

For each request record arrival, first-token time and every token time; compute TTFT, every inter-token gap (ITL), TPOT and E2E; output throughput = output tokens / makespan. Print p50/p99 TTFT, p50/p99/max ITL, throughput and preemptions for λ in {0.10, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40} under all four policies, with the realised arrival rate (requests ÷ the last arrival time) beside each λ: the seeded sample arrives 12% faster than λ (its 300 exponential draws sum to 267.3, not 300), a reminder that a short load test's offered load is itself random; plot fig-10-17 and save batching.png.

capacity(policy): bisect λ between 0.01 and 4.0 requests/s to a tolerance of 0.005 to find the highest rate at which p99 TTFT ≤ 3 s and p99 ITL ≤ 100 ms (on-demand admission, 256-token chunks); print the rate, the requests per hour (λ × 3,600) and the output throughput at that rate, from which costs are computed (Exercise e15 reuses it). Preparation value for the 24 GB card: 0.22 requests/s (about 790 an hour), 423 output tokens/s.
expected_observations: Static batching saturates near 300 output tokens/s, and its median TTFT is already about 13 s at 0.1 requests/s, because each batch holds the GPU until its longest request ends.

Continuous batching saturates near 560 tokens/s with reserve-max admission and near 590 with on-demand admission: about 0.34 requests/s or 1,220 an hour for Lab 3's shorter outputs, close to s11's estimate of 1,200 for 2,000-token outputs.
The knee lies between 0.25 and 0.30 requests/s: the median TTFT jumps from about 1.2 s to about 13 s (on-demand, no chunking).

On-demand admission lowers the TTFT tail below saturation (p99 2.9 s against 6.4 s at 0.20 requests/s). Combined with chunked prefill it over-commits past saturation, because requests still prefilling hold little cache when the next is admitted, and thrashes: hundreds of preemptions at 0.35-0.40 requests/s.
Chunked prefill removes the long stalls (maximum ITL from about 2.3 s to about 66 ms) at the price of a higher p99 ITL (about 62 ms against 18 ms), because more iterations carry prefill work.

Under the SLO the 24 GB card sustains about 0.22 requests/s (about 790 an hour) and 423 output tokens/s: goodput is about 70% of the saturation throughput. All values are from the prototype; the simulator is deterministic, so the lab's own output should match them closely.
extensions: Switch to an 8-bit cache (kv = 73,728) and repeat; then simulate the 80 GB, 3.35 TB/s card.
Make static batching memory-aware: cap each batch so that its cache fits in the 16 GB budget (10 requests at the worst case of 10,000 tokens each) and see how much further it falls behind.
Disaggregation: give prefill and decode separate simulated GPUs and compare p99 ITL.

Stress the tail: add a 5% share of 30,000-token prompts (the first 'What goes wrong' item), or replace Poisson arrivals by bursts of 10 requests every 50 s at the same mean rate, and watch p99 TTFT and the preemptions.

labs.title: Quantisation from scratch: weights, outliers and activations
labs.goal: Quantise SmolLM2-135M's linear layers with the schemes of s7, measure the damage as perplexity, find the activation outliers of s8, and repair simulated W8A8 with SmoothQuant.
labs.data: HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M (269 MB, shared with Labs 2, 5 and 6) and the WikiText-2 raw test split from the Salesforce/wikitext dataset repository, one parquet file of 0.73 MB.
steps: Load SmolLM2-135M in float32. Download wikitext-2-raw-v1/test-00000-of-00001.parquet (0.73 MB) with hf_hub_download(repo_type='dataset'); join the 'text' column; tokenise (301,948 tokens). Evaluation set: the first 8 windows of 512 tokens (4,096 tokens); calibration set: 4 windows from token 200,000 (disjoint). QUICK = True uses 4 evaluation windows.
perplexity(model) = exp of the mean next-token cross-entropy over the evaluation windows, batch 4. Print the float32 value: 20.85 on the preparation machine.

Write the quantisers from scratch: absmax per-tensor, absmax per-channel (per output row), absmax group-wise and zero-point group-wise with g = 64 (the hidden size 576 is not a multiple of 128). Apply them to the 210 nn.Linear layers of the 30 decoder layers (106,168,320 of 134,515,008 parameters), leaving the tied embedding and output matrix in float32. This is fake quantisation: weights are quantised and immediately dequantised, so the rounding error is real but no memory is saved; print each scheme's bits per weight and the size the quantised layers would occupy.

For each scheme print the mean relative weight error ‖W − Ŵ‖/‖W‖ and the perplexity, restoring the original weights between schemes. Preparation values: int8 per-tensor 0.029 and 21.57; int8 per-channel 0.0085 and 21.04; int4 per-tensor 0.49 and about 5.8×10⁶; int4 per-channel 0.155 and 48.4; int4 group-64 0.114 and 29.5; int4 group-64 zero-point 0.095 and 27.4.

Outlier hunt: forward pre-hooks record, for every linear layer, the per-input-channel maximum |x| over the calibration windows. Print the worst layer by max/median ratio (preparation machine: layers.11.mlp.down_proj, maximum 2,488 against a median channel of 1.27, ratio about 1,960), the median ratio over all layers (about 8.6), and for comparison the worst per-input-channel max/median ratio of the weights (about 12).

Simulated W8A8: int8 per-channel weights plus per-tensor dynamic int8 activations (a pre-hook quantises and dequantises each linear layer's input on every call). Perplexity 40.7 on the preparation machine.

SmoothQuant: for each layer s_j = max|X_j|^α / max|W_{:,j}|^(1−α) from the calibration statistics; quantise W·diag(s) per channel and X/s per tensor (the division happens in the hook here; a real implementation folds it into the preceding RMSNorm weight). α = 0.5: 26.4; α = 0.8: 24.6.
Plot perplexity (log scale) against bits per weight for every scheme and save quant.png (fig-10-11).
expected_observations: Per-tensor int4 is catastrophic: a few large weights set the scale and most weights round to zero.
Granularity buys most of the quality: per-channel, then group-wise; a zero-point helps further at 4 bits.
Eight bits per channel costs almost nothing (about +0.2 perplexity).

A few activation channels are hundreds to thousands of times the median while weights stay within about 12 times; per-tensor activation quantisation nearly doubles perplexity even at 8 bits, and SmoothQuant recovers most of the loss.
A 135M model is far more fragile than the 7B+ models of the GPTQ and AWQ papers, as the source's rule about small models predicts.
extensions: AWQ-lite: for each layer, choose α in {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1} for weight-only int4 group-64 with input-channel scales s = mean|X_j|^α, picking α by the layer's output error on the calibration activations; compare the perplexity with plain group-64.
Mixed precision: keep the down-projection layers in int8 and the rest in int4; compare perplexity and average bits per weight.
Task-level check: greedy-complete 20 short factual prompts with float32 and with int4 group-64 and count the answers that change.
Repeat steps 3-4 on SmolLM2-360M (724 MB, Lab 5's target model) and compare the damage with the 135M model.

labs.title: Speculative decoding from scratch
labs.goal: Implement greedy speculative decoding with SmolLM2-135M drafting for SmolLM2-360M, check that it reproduces the target's output, measure the acceptance rate and speed-up against the s9 formulas, and verify the sampling theorem numerically.
labs.data: HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M (724 MB) and HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M (269 MB, already downloaded in Lab 2). The two share one 49,152-token tokenizer.
steps: Load SmolLM2-135M (draft) and SmolLM2-360M (target) in float32 and one tokenizer; print the parameter counts, 134,515,008 and 361,821,120.

Measure step costs on a cached 20-token prefix (median of 20 repeats, cropping the cache back after each): a draft one-token step, a target one-token step and target verifications of γ + 1 = 3, 5 and 7 tokens. Print c = t_draft/t_target and v_γ = t_verify(γ + 1)/t_target for γ = 2, 4 and 6. Preparation machine (shared with other jobs): 57 ms, 116 ms and 183 ms for the 5-token verification, so c ≈ 0.49 and v₄ ≈ 1.6. Verification costs depend on the machine's load (a later, quieter run gave c ≈ 0.45 and v ≈ 1.1-1.2, 1.1-1.25 and 1.2-1.35 for 3, 5 and 7 tokens), which is why the lab measures v for each γ.

greedy(model, ids, n): prefill, then one token per step with a transformers DynamicCache. Baseline: the target on 5 prompts (a sentence defining a safety case, 'The main steps of a hazard analysis and risk assessment are', a Python function header, a history sentence, a sentence on thermal runaway in a lithium-ion battery) × 64 new tokens; print tokens/s (about 8 on the preparation machine).

speculative(ids, n, γ): keep a cache for each model; in each iteration feed the draft the tokens it has not yet seen and draft γ tokens greedily; run the target once on [last token, γ drafts]; accept the longest prefix on which the draft equals the target's argmax; append the target's own token at the first mismatch (or the bonus token if all were accepted); crop both caches to the accepted length with DynamicCache.crop. Count accepted drafts, rejections and iterations.

For γ in {2, 4, 6} print α̂ = accepted / (accepted + rejections) to three decimals for that γ's run, the tokens per iteration measured and predicted by (1 − α̂^{γ+1})/(1 − α̂) with that γ's α̂, whether each output equals the baseline, the time, the measured speed-up, and the predicted speed-up E/(γc + v_γ) with step 2's c and v_γ. Preparation machine (5 prompts × 64 tokens): α̂ = 0.871, 0.865 and 0.874; tokens per iteration 2.64, 3.86 and 4.57 against 2.63, 3.82 and 4.84 predicted (one shared α̂ = 0.87 would give 2.63, 3.86 and 4.79); identical outputs on every prompt; speed-ups 0.95×, 1.22× and 1.14×. At γ = 4 the prediction is 3.82/(4 × 0.49 + 1.6) = 1.07×, so the measured speed-up is 14% above it.

Check the theorem for sampling: for the hazard-analysis prompt compute the target's p and the draft's q at temperature 1; simulate the acceptance rule 200,000 times in torch (sample x ~ q, accept with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), otherwise sample from the residual); print the empirical acceptance rate against Σ min(p, q) (0.8555 against 0.8553), the total-variation distance from the empirical distribution to p (0.016, sampling noise) and TV(q, p) (0.145), and the top-5 tokens' probabilities under p and empirically.
expected_observations: Greedy speculative decoding reproduces the target's greedy output exactly on every prompt tested; if a run ever differs, it differs at a near-tie, so print the top-2 logit gap at that position.
Tokens per iteration agree with (1 − α^{γ+1})/(1 − α) to within about 6%: the independence assumption is good enough.

On a CPU the speed-up is small (about 1.0-1.2×) because the draft costs half a target step and verification costs more than one step. The formula fed with the measured c and v predicts a speed-up near 1 (1.07× at γ = 4); the measured 1.22× is 14% higher, a reminder that step costs timed in isolation on a busy CPU are a rough guide. Speculation pays when the draft is 10-100 times cheaper and verification is bandwidth-bound, as on a GPU.
The sampled outputs follow p, not q: the residual step is what makes the method exact.
extensions: Prompt-lookup drafting: replace the draft model by copying the tokens that followed the last matching 3-gram in the context (c ≈ 0) and test it on a copy-heavy prompt such as 'Correct the spelling in the following paragraph: ...'; measure α and the speed-up.
Sampling-mode speculative decoding at temperature 0.8 with the full acceptance rule at every position.
Use the -Instruct versions of both models with a chat prompt and compare α.
Batch the target over the 5 prompts and watch the gain shrink as verification stops being free.

labs.title: Batched generation on a CPU: throughput and determinism
labs.goal: Run batched greedy generation with SmolLM2-135M at B = 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 in plain PyTorch, measure the prefill time, the decode step and the per-sequence and aggregate tokens/s, compare them with Lab 1's CPU roofline (the source's Exercise 2, done on a CPU), and test whether one request's output changes with the batch it runs in (the source's Exercise 3).
labs.data: HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M (269 MB; already cached if you ran Lab 2). No server software and no other download.
steps: Load SmolLM2-135M in float32 with its tokenizer; set tok.pad_token = tok.eos_token and tok.padding_side = 'left'; print the parameter count, 134,515,008. Define 16 short prompts (12-28 tokens: sentences about the pressure-relief valve, the hazard log and the safety case, plus a few general ones) and print their lengths.

batched_greedy(prompts, n_new=64): tokenise with padding; compute position ids from the attention mask (cumulative sum minus one, clipped at 0), so that a left-padded row starts at position 0 like an unpadded one; prefill with a transformers DynamicCache and time it (the TTFT of every request in the batch); then decode one token per step for all rows, appending a column of ones to the mask and advancing each row's position by one, timing every step with time.perf_counter(). Return the tokens, the prefill time, the step times and, optionally, one row's logits at every step.

For B in {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} (the first B prompts, after one warm-up call) print the prefill time, the median decode step (ms), per-sequence tokens/s = 1/step and aggregate tokens/s = B/step. Preparation machine (4 threads, a desktop shared with other jobs; two runs differed by up to 1.7×): prefill 43-81 ms at B = 1, rising to 0.49-0.59 s at B = 16 (448 padded prompt tokens); steps of 30-50 ms at B = 1 and 60-82 ms at B = 16; aggregate 20-33 tokens/s at B = 1 and 194-268 at B = 16, while each sequence slowed to 12-17 tokens/s.

Compare with Lab 1's roofline: enter the bandwidth and peak FLOP/s measured there (the preparation values were 12.6 GB/s and about 200 GFLOP/s) and predict each step as max((538 MB + B·46,080 B·ctx)/BW, (2·N_matmul·B + 4·L·d·ctx·B)/peak), with N_matmul = N = 134.5M (the embeddings are tied, so the shared matrix is the output head and every parameter takes part in a matrix multiplication), L = 30, d = 576 and 46,080 cache bytes per token in float32; print measured over predicted. The prediction stays near 43-46 ms and bandwidth-bound up to B = 16, because the float32 intensity (about B/2 FLOP/byte) is still below the CPU's ridge of about 16, while the measured step roughly doubles: on a CPU, small matrices and per-layer overheads, not bandwidth alone, set the cost of a batched step.
Plot per-sequence and aggregate tokens/s against B (log x) with the roofline predictions dashed; save batch.png.

Determinism: run the first prompt ('The pressure relief valve protects the reactor vessel from overpressure.', 12 tokens) alone and as row 0 of the first 8 prompts, where it is left-padded by 16 tokens; greedy, 64 new tokens; keep row 0's logits at every step. Print whether the tokens are identical, the largest absolute logit difference over the 64 steps, and the smallest top-2 logit gap of the solo run with its step. Preparation machine (the same in both runs, because it does not depend on load): tokens identical; largest difference 4.8×10⁻⁵ (median 3.6×10⁻⁵); smallest top-2 gap 0.056 at step 22, about 1,000 times the difference.
expected_observations: Prefill time grows roughly with the number of prompt tokens in the batch, while the decode step grows far more slowly than B: aggregate throughput rises 8-10 times from B = 1 to 16 while each sequence slows by a factor of 1.6-2 (s5, fig-10-7, on a real model).

The roofline predicts an almost flat, bandwidth-bound step, but the measured step rises faster with B: on a CPU, small matrix products and per-layer overheads make batching less free than on a GPU. The roofline is a floor, not a forecast.

The same prompt gives identical tokens alone and in a batch of 8, and its logits differ by about 10⁻⁵ (float32 reduction order changes with the batch's shape); the smallest top-2 gap in 64 tokens is about a thousand times larger, so nothing flips here. Batch-dependent numerics are real but need a near-tie inside the noise to change a token; lower precision, longer outputs and many requests make such ties likely, which is why s13 says to test reproducibility rather than assume it.
extensions: Repeat the determinism test in bfloat16 (slow on many CPUs) and with 512 new tokens; report the first differing position, if any, and the top-2 gap there.

norun (needs software and a download outside this lab; no main-text number depends on it): serve Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct as a 491 MB GGUF file (q4_k_m) with llama.cpp's llama-server or with Ollama, write a streaming client with urllib and json that records TTFT and every inter-token gap from the server-sent events, load-test it at concurrency 1, 2, 4 and 8, and compare with this lab's batch curve.

norun (GPU; the source's Exercise 2): with vLLM and a 7-9B 4-bit model on any GPU or Colab, measure TTFT and tokens/s at batch 1, 4, 16 and 64 with 1,000-token prompts, plot throughput against batch, and compare the saturation point with Lab 1's prediction for that card.

exercises.prompt: A colleague estimates the single-user decode speed of a 9B model in bf16 on a GPU with 989 TFLOP/s and 3.35 TB/s as 989×10¹² / (2 × 9×10⁹) ≈ 55,000 tokens/s. What is wrong with the estimate, and what is the right order of magnitude?
exercises.solution_sketch: At batch 1 decode is bandwidth-bound (intensity about 1 FLOP/byte against a ridge of 295). Each token reads about 18 GB of bf16 weights: 18 GB / 3.35 TB/s ≈ 5.4 ms, about 185 tokens/s, and less once the cache and achieved bandwidth are counted. The FLOP-based figure is an aggregate ceiling reached only at a batch of about 300, not the speed one user sees.

exercises.prompt: Derive the arithmetic intensity of Y = WX for W ∈ R^{m×n} stored at b_w bytes per element and X ∈ R^{n×B}, Y ∈ R^{m×B} at b_a bytes per element, and show that it is about 2B/b_w when B ≪ m, n. Using Section 4's datasheet figures: (a) with bf16 weights and activations on the A100 (312 TFLOP/s, 2.04 TB/s), at what B does the product become compute-bound? (b) With int8 weights (b_w = 1) and bf16 activations on the L40S (362 TFLOP/s, 0.864 TB/s)? (c) Why do these batch sizes overstate what a server reaches at long context?
exercises.solution_sketch: FLOPs 2mnB; bytes b_w·mn + b_a·B(m + n); I = 2mnB / (b_w·mn + b_a·B(m + n)) → 2B/b_w when B(m + n) ≪ mn. (a) Ridge 312/2.04 = 153 FLOP/byte; 2B/2 = 153, so B ≈ 153. (b) Ridge 362/0.864 = 419; 2B/1 = 419, so B ≈ 210: halving the weight bytes doubles the intensity at every B. (For m = n = 4,096 the exact formula gives about 165 and 263, because B is no longer much smaller than m and n.) (c) Each sequence also reads its own KV cache, whose intensity, 2(n_h/n_kv)/b, does not grow with B; at long context these reads keep the step bandwidth-bound well past these batch sizes, and memory capacity usually runs out first (18 sequences for the case study on 24 GB).

exercises.prompt: From their configuration files, SmolLM2-135M has num_hidden_layers 30, hidden_size 576, num_attention_heads 9 and num_key_value_heads 3; SmolLM2-360M has 32, 960, 15 and 5; Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct has 24, 896, 14 and 2. Compute each model's KV cache per token in bf16 and in int8, and for one 8,192-token sequence in bf16. Which has the smallest cache per token, and why, although it has the most parameters?
exercises.solution_sketch: d_head = hidden_size / num_attention_heads = 64 for all three. Per token in bf16: 2·30·3·64·2 = 23,040 B; 2·32·5·64·2 = 40,960 B; 2·24·2·64·2 = 12,288 B; int8 halves each (11,520; 20,480; 6,144). For 8,192 tokens: 188.7 MB, 335.5 MB and 100.7 MB. Qwen2.5-0.5B is smallest: 2 KV heads for 14 query heads (groups of 7) and 24 layers. Its larger parameter count sits largely in its 151,936-entry embedding table (136M parameters), which costs nothing in the cache.

exercises.prompt: Grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads for 32 query heads cuts the case study's cache by a factor of 4. Explain why it does not cut the attention FLOPs, why it nevertheless speeds up decode at long context, and what it may cost.
exercises.solution_sketch: Every query head still scores t keys and averages t values, so the FLOPs are unchanged. Decode attention is bandwidth-bound (intensity 2(n_h/n_kv)/b), so reading four times fewer key and value bytes makes it about four times faster and leaves room for four times as many sequences. Sharing keys and values across heads reduces capacity slightly; GQA was shown to come close to multi-head quality (Ainslie et al. 2023), and models are trained with it from the start.

exercises.prompt: A server reserves the maximum length (8,192 tokens) of cache for every request. Name the kinds of waste this creates and say which of them paged allocation removes. With blocks of b tokens, how much waste remains per sequence, and why do engines not simply use 1-token blocks?
exercises.solution_sketch: Slots reserved but never used (most requests end well before 8,192 tokens), the unused tail inside each allocation, and gaps between allocations of different sizes. Paging allocates blocks on demand from one pool, so reservations and gaps disappear; what remains is the unused part of each sequence's last block: at most b − 1 tokens and about b/2 on average, a few MB for the case study with 16-token blocks against about 1 GB for an 8,192-token reservation. Smaller blocks cut that waste further but lengthen every block table and split each sequence's keys and values into more, smaller pieces, which the attention kernel gathers with less efficient memory reads; the vLLM paper studies the trade-off and uses 16 tokens by default.

exercises.prompt: Each request to the safety-case assistant is assembled from (a) a line 'Request time: <timestamp>', (b) a 2,500-token system prompt, (c) a 1,200-token excerpt of a standard that is the same for all users of one project, and (d) the user's question of about 100 tokens, in that order. Reorder the parts to maximise prefix-cache hits, and say how many prompt tokens per request can then skip prefill, with 16-token blocks.
exercises.solution_sketch: Order b, c, d, a (or move the timestamp into the user turn). The system prompt is shared by every request and b + c (3,700 tokens) by every request of one project, so up to 3,696 tokens (231 full blocks) skip prefill. In the original order the timestamp differs on every request, so the first block never matches and nothing is reused.

exercises.prompt: Two int4 schemes for the case study's 8.305×10⁹ block weights: (a) groups of 128 with an fp16 scale and an fp16 zero-point, 4.25 bits per weight (4.41 GB); (b) groups of 32 with an fp16 scale only, 4.5 bits per weight (4.67 GB). Which would you expect to be more accurate on a model with outlier weights, and why? What does (a)'s zero-point buy that (b) lacks?
exercises.solution_sketch: (b), usually: an outlier stretches the scale of its own group only, and (b)'s groups hold 32 weights instead of 128, so four times fewer weights lose resolution to each outlier (s7's outlier example). (a)'s zero-point lets a skewed group use all 16 levels, which a symmetric grid wastes on the side the values do not reach; it does not help against an outlier, which still sets the range of its group. The 0.26 GB that (b) costs buys granularity; Lab 4 compares group-64 with and without a zero-point.

exercises.prompt: Quantise w = (0.62, −0.11, 0.05, −0.90, 0.33, 0.07, −0.25, 0.48) to int4 (a) with symmetric absmax (q in [−7, 7]) and (b) with min-max zero-point (q in [0, 15]). Give q, ŵ and the RMS error for each. (c) Replace 0.05 by 4.5 and repeat (a): what happens to the other seven weights?

Prove that speculative sampling (draw x ~ q; accept with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)); on rejection draw from r(x) = max(0, p(x) − q(x)) / Σ_y max(0, p(y) − q(y))) emits x with probability exactly p(x). Show that the probability of acceptance is Σ_x min(p(x), q(x)) = 1 − TV(p, q). Check both on p = (0.55, 0.25, 0.15, 0.05) and q = (0.30, 0.40, 0.10, 0.20).

With a per-token acceptance rate α, independent across positions, derive the expected number of tokens per speculative iteration with draft length γ. For α = 0.75 and a draft costing c = 0.1 of a target step (verification costing one step), tabulate the speed-up for γ = 1 to 6 and find the best γ. Repeat for c = 0.3, and say what the two results imply for choosing a draft model.
exercises.solution_sketch: P(at least k accepted) = α^k for k ≤ γ, so E[tokens] = 1 + Σ_{k=1}^{γ} α^k = (1 − α^{γ+1})/(1 − α): 1.75, 2.31, 2.73, 3.05, 3.29, 3.47 for γ = 1...6. With c = 0.1, S = E/(γc + 1) = 1.59, 1.93, 2.10, 2.18, 2.19, 2.17: best γ = 5 at 2.19×, with a flat optimum from 4 to 6. With c = 0.3, S = 1.35, 1.45, 1.44, 1.39, 1.32, 1.24: best γ = 2 at 1.45×, and from γ = 10 speculation is slower than plain decoding. A draft that costs a third of a target step caps the gain near 1.5× however long it drafts, and the dearer the draft, the shorter its best draft length; useful drafts are 10-100 times cheaper than the target. Lab 5's CPU draft, with c ≈ 0.5, sits in the second regime.

exercises.prompt: Redo the sizing table of s11 (24, 48 and 80 GB cards, 2.5 GB runtime overhead, 6,000-token requests, bf16 cache) for (a) a 14B-class model at 8 bits (14 GB of weights; L = 48, n_kv = 8, d_head = 128) and (b) a 1B-class model in bf16 (2.4 GB; L = 16, n_kv = 8, d_head = 64). Give the concurrent requests on each card and the single-stream decode bound from the weights alone on a 1.0 TB/s card.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) 196,608 B per token, 1.18 GB per request; free memory 7.5, 31.5 and 63.5 GB, so 6, 26 and 53 requests; 14 GB / 1.0 TB/s = 14 ms, about 71 tokens/s. (b) 32,768 B per token, 0.197 GB per request; free 19.1, 43.1 and 75.1 GB, so 97, 219 and 381 requests; 2.4 ms, about 417 tokens/s. The 14B model is limited by memory; the 1B model reaches the limits of compute and scheduling long before its cache fills.

exercises.prompt: An agent makes 20 sequential model calls per task. Section 12 showed that if each call independently exceeds its p99 latency with probability 0.01, 18% of tasks contain at least one slow call. On what should a team that runs such agents set its latency SLO, and why is a per-call p99 the wrong target?
exercises.solution_sketch: A per-call p99 event is a typical event for a 20-call task, so a per-call p99 SLO says little about what users experience. Set the SLO on the task-level latency users see, end to end over the whole chain, or on a much higher per-call percentile (p99.9, which a 20-call task exceeds in about 2% of tasks); and work on the tail itself (hedged requests, as Dean and Barroso describe; admission control; chunked prefill).

exercises.prompt: Two runs of the same request at temperature 0 give different answers on a busy server and identical answers on an idle one. Explain the mechanism, why the difference starts at one token and then grows, and what a reproducibility test should record.
exercises.solution_sketch: Kernels choose reduction orders by batch shape, and floating-point addition is not associative, so the logits differ in the last bits with the batch's composition. Where the top two logits are within that noise the argmax flips; every later token is conditioned on a different prefix, so the outputs diverge from there. A test should compare runs alone and under load and record the first differing position, the top-2 logit gap there and the batch conditions; acceptance should rest on checks, not byte equality.

exercises.prompt: Suppose the 24 GB card of Section 11 can be rented for an assumed USD 0.80 per hour (a lower quote than the section's USD 1.00; both are assumptions, as of 2026) and sustains 2.4 million output tokens per hour at full load. (a) What does a million output tokens cost at 100% and at 25% utilisation? (b) Above what utilisation is the card cheaper per output token than a hosted model charging USD 0.80 per million output tokens (Module 07's assumed price) at equal quality on your task? (c) Name two costs this comparison leaves out.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) USD 0.80 / 2.4 = USD 0.33 per million at full load; at 25% the card yields 0.6 million tokens per paid hour, USD 1.33 per million. (b) The break-even utilisation u solves 0.80 / (2.4u) = 0.80, so u = 0.80 / (2.4 × 0.80) = 0.42: above 42% the card is cheaper. (c) Engineering and operations time; redundant or fallback capacity; evaluation runs after every model change; and, on the hosted side, the price of input tokens (USD 0.20 per million in Module 07's assumption), which favours the card. Utilisation dominates: an idle GPU still costs its hourly price.

exercises.prompt: A capacity plan under an SLO. Extend Lab 3's simulator: use capacity() to find the highest arrival rate at which p99 TTFT ≤ 3 s and p99 ITL ≤ 100 ms hold (300 requests, Lab 3's workload, on-demand cache admission, 256-token prefill budget per iteration) for (a) the 24 GB, 1.0 TB/s card with a bf16 cache, (b) the same card with an 8-bit cache, (c) an 80 GB card with 3.35 TB/s and 989 TFLOP/s, and (d) a 24 GB card with 0.30 TB/s and 121 TFLOP/s. Convert each rate to requests per hour and, from the printed output throughput at assumed prices of USD 1.00, 1.00, 2.50 and 0.80 per hour (assumptions, as of 2026; the 80 GB card's is Module 07's H100 price), to cost per million output tokens. Which card is cheapest per token under the SLO, and how does that compare with ranking the cards by hourly price?
exercises.solution_sketch: Prototype results (bisection, seeded workload): (a) about 0.22 requests/s (about 790 an hour), 423 output tokens/s, USD 0.66 per million; (b) about 0.25 requests/s (about 900 an hour), 482 tokens/s, USD 0.58 per million; (c) about 2.19 requests/s (about 7,900 an hour), 3,497 tokens/s, USD 0.20 per million; (d) about 0.065 requests/s (about 230 an hour), 124 tokens/s, USD 1.79 per million. Costs come from the printed throughput (price per hour ÷ output tokens per hour × 10⁶), not from λ times an assumed output length: the seeded sample arrives about 12% faster than λ, so throughput ÷ λ is about 1,920 tokens although the mean output is 1,737. The most expensive card per hour is the cheapest per token under the SLO, because its bandwidth, memory and compute all scale; the cheapest card per hour is the most expensive per token. An 8-bit cache is the cheapest single improvement on the 24 GB card. Answers within about 20% are fine: they depend on the seed and the bisection tolerance.

quiz.question: The case-study model's 5.5 GB 4-bit file runs on a GPU with 1.0 TB/s of bandwidth and 165 TFLOP/s. Its batch-1 decode speed is closest to:
quiz.explanation: Decode at batch 1 is bandwidth-bound: 5.5 GB / 1.0 TB/s = 5.5 ms per token, about 180 tokens/s. About 9,000 tokens/s is the compute bound 165×10¹² / (2 × 8.93×10⁹) = 9,240, reachable only as an aggregate at large batch; the other two options are off by a factor of ten.

quiz.question: A model has L = 32 layers, 8 KV heads and a head dimension of 128. Its KV cache per token in bf16 is:
quiz.explanation: 2 (K and V) × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes. 65,536 forgets either the factor 2 for K and V or the 2 bytes per value; 524,288 is the multi-head figure with 32 KV heads; 32,768 drops both factors of 2.

quiz.question: Which statement about batching decode is correct?
options: Batching shortens each sequence's time per step.
Batching amortises both the weight reads and the KV-cache reads across sequences.
Batching amortises the weight reads but not each sequence's KV-cache reads, so at long context the gain flattens.
quiz.explanation: All sequences in a step share one read of the weights, but each reads its own cache, whose intensity does not grow with the batch. Per-sequence step time rises with the batch, it does not shorten; and decode is precisely where batching helps most.

quiz.question: The main advantage of continuous batching over static batching is that:
options: finished sequences leave and waiting ones join at every step, so slots do not sit idle until the longest sequence ends
it removes the need for a KV cache
it guarantees a lower TTFT at any load
quiz.explanation: Iteration-level scheduling refills slots as they free. It still needs the cache; prefill is compute-bound anyway; and past saturation TTFT grows without bound under any policy.

quiz.question: Prefix caching never hits on your service. The most likely cause is:
options: the GPU has too little bandwidth
the cache is stored in 8 bits
the system prompt begins with a per-request timestamp
quiz.explanation: A hit needs an identical token prefix; a value that changes at the top of the prompt makes the first block differ, so nothing after it can match. Bandwidth, GQA and cache precision do not affect matching.

quiz.question: Quantising SmolLM2-135M's linear weights to int4 with one absmax scale per tensor gave a perplexity in the millions, while groups of 64 gave about 29. Why?
options: a few large weights set the scale, so most weights round to zero; groups confine each outlier's effect
quiz.explanation: With one scale per tensor the largest magnitude sets the step size, and the bulk of small weights falls into the zero bin. Symmetric int4 does represent negatives; per-tensor scales use fewer bits, not more; and round-to-nearest needs no calibration.

quiz.question: Weight-only int4 quantisation mainly speeds up:
options: prefill of long prompts, because it reduces FLOPs
decode at small batch, because it reduces the bytes read per step
quiz.explanation: Weights are dequantised to fp16 for the multiplication, so the FLOPs are unchanged and compute-bound prefill gains nothing; bandwidth-bound decode reads a quarter of the bf16 bytes and speeds up accordingly, besides saving memory.

quiz.question: In speculative sampling the draft model is poor (acceptance rate 0.3). The output distribution is:
options: a mixture of the target and draft distributions weighted by the acceptance rate
the target's only under greedy decoding
exactly the target's; the poor draft only lowers the speed-up
quiz.explanation: The acceptance test plus residual resampling gives min(p, q) + (p − min(p, q)) = p for any q. The draft affects how many tokens each target pass yields, never which distribution they come from.

quiz.question: With acceptance rate α = 0.8 and draft length γ = 4, the expected number of tokens per target forward pass is:
quiz.explanation: (1 − 0.8⁵)/(1 − 0.8) = 3.36. 3.2 = γα ignores the truncation at the first rejection and the extra token every iteration yields; 4 assumes every draft is accepted with no extra token; 5 assumes all are accepted plus the bonus token every time.

quiz.question: SmoothQuant makes int8 activation quantisation work by:
options: dividing each activation channel by s_j and multiplying the matching weight row by s_j, which leaves XW unchanged and moves range from activations to weights
clipping activation outliers to a percentile
keeping the outlier channels in fp16
retraining the model with quantisation in the loop
quiz.explanation: The per-channel rescaling is an exact identity on the product and is folded into the previous layer. Keeping outliers in fp16 is LLM.int8()'s decomposition; retraining is quantisation-aware training; clipping changes the function.

quiz.question: At moderate load your p50 TTFT is 0.4 s but p99 is 9 s, while TPOT is normal. The most plausible cause and remedy are:
options: too little bandwidth; buy a faster GPU
requests queueing behind long prefills near the knee; chunked prefill, admission control or more capacity
quiz.explanation: A normal TPOT rules out a bandwidth problem in decode; a long TTFT tail at moderate load is queueing, made worse by long prompts' prefills. Cache precision and temperature do not change waiting time.

quiz.question: A server completes 0.33 requests/s, and each request spends 55 s in the system on average. By Little's law the average number of requests in the system is:
quiz.explanation: L = λW = 0.33 × 55 ≈ 18, the case study's cache limit on the 24 GB card. 167 = W/λ and 0.006 = λ/W divide instead of multiplying; 55 ignores the arrival rate.

papers.citation: Kwon, W. et al., "Efficient memory management for large language model serving with PagedAttention." SOSP, 2023.
papers.why: The paper behind vLLM: a clear account of why the KV cache, not compute, limits serving, and how operating-system paging fixes it. Short sections, informative figures.
papers.read: Read the introduction, the section on memory challenges in LLM serving (with its figure of KV-cache usage in existing systems), and the method sections on PagedAttention, the KV cache manager, decoding with PagedAttention, other decoding scenarios (parallel sampling, beam search) and scheduling and preemption. Skim the first evaluation figures. Skip distributed execution, the implementation details and the ablations.
questions: What share of KV-cache memory held actual token states in the systems the authors measured, and which kinds of waste account for the rest?
Draw the block table for a 70-token sequence with 16-token blocks: how many physical blocks does it use and how many slots are empty? (5 and 10.)

How does copy-on-write make 4 parallel samples of one 1,000-token prompt cheaper, and how many blocks does the prompt part need with and without sharing? (66 against 252 with 16-token blocks, counting a copy of the partly filled last block for three of the samples.)
When the GPU runs out of blocks, what are the two preemption strategies, and when is recomputation cheaper than swapping?

papers.citation: Lin, J. et al., "AWQ: Activation-aware weight quantization for LLM compression and acceleration." MLSys, 2024.
papers.why: The clearest statement of why activation statistics, not weight magnitudes, decide which weights matter, with an error argument a reader can redo in a few lines; it connects Lab 4's outliers with the 4-bit files people actually serve.
papers.read: Read the introduction and the method section: preserving the 1% of salient weights, protecting them by activation-aware scaling (the error analysis), and the search for the scaling factor. Skim the main perplexity table. Skip the inference-system section.
questions: Why are salient channels selected by activation magnitude rather than by weight magnitude, and which experiment shows it?
Reproduce the error argument: why does scaling a channel by s > 1 before quantisation reduce its relative rounding error by about 1/s, and what limits how large s can be?
What does AWQ search over, with what objective, and why does it need no back-propagation?
Relate α in AWQ's s = s_X^α to α in SmoothQuant and in Lab 4's SmoothQuant step.

papers.citation: Leviathan, Y., Kalman, M., Matias, Y., "Fast inference from transformers via speculative decoding." ICML, 2023.
papers.why: The original statement of speculative sampling with the correctness proof and the walltime analysis that s9 derives; short and self-contained.
papers.read: Read the introduction, the method section (standard sampling with the speculative rule) and the analysis of the number of generated tokens, the walltime improvement and the choice of γ; read the correctness proof in the appendix and Section 4.2 on the acceptance rates of different drafts. Skim the experiments' tables. Skip the arithmetic-operations analysis on a first reading.
questions: The paper defines a divergence between the draft and target distributions. Show that it equals the total-variation distance and that the acceptance probability is one minus it.
Re-derive the expected number of tokens per iteration. Which independence assumption does it make, and how well did that assumption hold in Lab 5?
The walltime result assumes verifying γ + 1 tokens costs one target step. When is that false, and how does Lab 5's measured v change the prediction?

Section 4.2 reports acceptance rates for very cheap drafts, down to a bigram model. What speed-up does a draft with c ≈ 0 and α ≈ 0.2 give at best, however long it drafts, and why does Table 2 nevertheless favour a small transformer draft? What does that say about trading a draft's cost against its acceptance rate?

widgets.name: serving-calculator
widgets.teaching_point: Memory capacity sets how many sequences fit, bandwidth sets how long each decode step takes, and the batch trades each user's speed for total throughput; at long contexts the cache reads, not the weights, dominate the step.

widgets.defaults: Case study 9.5B, 4-bit, bf16 cache, prompt 4,000, output 2,000, B = 18, the 24 GB 1.0 TB/s card, overhead 2.5 GB, MFU 0.5, bandwidth fraction 1.0. The readouts then show 5.5 GB of weights, 147,456 B per token, 0.885 GB per sequence, a maximum of 18 sequences, TTFT 0.92 s, a decode step of 18.8 ms (bandwidth-bound), 53 tokens/s per sequence and about 960 aggregate: the s11 numbers. Switching the cache to 8 bits doubles the maximum to 36; switching the card to the L4 class leaves 18 but cuts the speed by 3.3; switching the weights to bf16 (19.10 GB) leaves room for 2 sequences.
widgets.spec: All arithmetic in decimal units (GB = 10⁹ bytes, TB/s = 10¹² bytes/s, TFLOP/s = 10¹² FLOP/s). weights = 5.5 × 10⁹ for the case-study preset at '4-bit', otherwise params × 10⁹ × bits / 8 (bits = 4.125 for '4-bit'). kv_tok = 2 × L × n_kv × d_head × kv_bytes. T_full = prompt + output (memory per sequence); t_mean = prompt + output / 2 (mean context during decode). free = mem × 10⁹ − weights − overhead × 10⁹. max_conc = floor(free / (kv_tok × T_full)), or 0 with the message 'weights and overhead exceed memory' if free ≤ 0 (then disable the chart). ttft = (2 × matmul_params × 10⁹ × prompt + 2 × L × d × prompt²) / (mfu × tflops × 10¹²). For any B: t_mem(B) = (weights + B × kv_tok × t_mean) / (bw × 10¹² × bw_frac); t_cmp(B) = (2 × matmul_params × 10⁹ × B + 4 × L × d × t_mean × B) / (tflops × 10¹²); t(B) = max(t_mem, t_cmp); per-sequence = 1/t(B); aggregate = B/t(B); output time = output × t(B). The chart evaluates B = 1...512 on a log grid of about 100 points. When B > max_conc, still compute and display, but colour the readouts amber and label them 'does not fit'. Presets fill the custom fields, and editing any field (the total or matmul parameters included) switches the preset to 'Custom', after which '4-bit' means 4.125 bits per weight for every parameter. The widget deliberately ignores the embedding-read refinement, tensor parallelism and prefill interference; say so in a one-line caption. Render with vanilla JS and SVG; recompute on every input event; keep the layout usable at 400 px width by stacking the controls above the chart.

widgets.name: speculative-speedup
widgets.teaching_point: The speed-up of speculative decoding is set by the acceptance rate and the draft's relative cost, with an optimal draft length beyond which drafts waste work, while the output distribution stays exactly the target's because the rejection step resamples the residual.
controls: slider: acceptance rate α, 0.00-0.99, step 0.01, default 0.80
slider: draft length γ, 1-16, integer, default 4
slider: draft cost ratio c, 0.00-1.00, step 0.01, default 0.05
slider: verification cost v in target steps, 1.0-3.0, step 0.1, default 1.0
panel B: two editable 4-bar distributions p (target) and q (draft) whose bar tops can be dragged; values renormalise to sum to 1; defaults p = (0.50, 0.30, 0.15, 0.05), q = (0.40, 0.40, 0.10, 0.10)
displays: panel A, bar chart of P(tokens per iteration = k) for k = 1...γ+1: P(k) = α^(k−1)(1 − α) for k ≤ γ and P(γ + 1) = α^γ, with the mean marked
panel A, line chart of the speed-up S(γ') = (1 − α^(γ'+1)) / ((1 − α)(γ'c + v)) for γ' = 1...16, the current γ highlighted, the best γ' marked, and a horizontal line at S = 1 labelled 'no gain'
panel A readouts: expected tokens per iteration; speed-up; best γ and its speed-up; drafted tokens wasted per iteration, γ − α(1 − α^γ)/(1 − α)

panel B: bars of p and q side by side, the overlap min(p, q) shaded, α = Σ min(p, q) and TV = 1 − α printed, the residual distribution (p − min(p, q))/(1 − α), and the output distribution min(p, q) + (1 − α)·residual drawn over p to show they coincide; after 'simulate', the empirical histogram beside p with the total-variation distance printed (below 0.01 at the defaults)
widgets.defaults: α = 0.80, γ = 4, c = 0.05, v = 1: expected tokens 3.36, speed-up 2.80, best γ = 8 at 3.09, so the reader sees diminishing returns at once. Panel B defaults give α = 0.85, TV = 0.15 and residual (2/3, 0, 1/3, 0), the s9 worked example.
widgets.spec: E(γ) = (1 − α^(γ+1)) / (1 − α) for α < 1, and γ + 1 at α = 1 (the limit; clamp the slider at 0.99 but compute the limit if α is set programmatically). S(γ) = E(γ) / (γc + v). With c = 0, S = E/v. Wasted drafts = γ − (E(γ) − 1). The best γ' is the argmax of S over 1...16; on ties take the smaller. Panel B: when the user drags a bar, set it to the pointer's value in [0, 1] and rescale the other three proportionally so the total is 1 (if the other three are all zero, share the remainder equally); recompute min(p, q), α, the residual and the output. If α = 1 (p = q), show 'no residual needed' instead of dividing by zero. A token with q = 0 is never drafted, so its acceptance ratio is not displayed. The simulation draws x from q, accepts with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), otherwise draws from the residual, over 10,000 steps using a seeded generator (for example mulberry32 with seed 1) so the result is repeatable, then shows the histogram and TV. Render with vanilla JS and SVG; panels stack vertically below 600 px width.

writer_notes:
RUNNING CASE STUDY (use these numbers everywhere; Module 07 owns the configuration and the workload, s11 owns the serving derivation). A hypothetical team adapts an open-weight bilingual (English-Chinese) model of about 9.5B parameters, released in base and instruct versions, to draft and check safety-case arguments for the pressure-relief system of a reactor vessel: Module 07 chooses it; Module 08 costs its continued pretraining on domain text; Module 09 post-trains it and merges the LoRA adapter into bf16 weights; this module quantises, re-evaluates, hashes and serves that merged artifact. Never present it as a real model, product or plan. Call the domain 'safety-case arguments' and the output a 'hazard log' (not 'safety-assurance arguments', 'HARA' or 'hazard table'). Configuration (Module 07): L = 36, d = 4,096, 32 query heads and 8 KV heads of d_head = 128, SwiGLU with d_ff = 15,360, vocabulary 152,064, untied embeddings. Per layer 230,694,912 parameters (attention 41,943,040; feed-forward 188,743,680; norms 8,192); all blocks 8,305,016,832; embedding and output head 622,854,144 each; N = 9,550,729,216 ('9.5B'); N_matmul = N − V·d = 8,927,875,072 (8.93×10⁹). FLOP AND MEMORY CONVENTION (Module 06 owns it; s1 recalls it once and does not re-derive the attention term): memory uses N; a forward token costs 2·N_matmul FLOPs (1.79×10¹⁰) plus 4·L·d·t of attention at context t, which sums to about 2·L·d·T² over a causal prompt; 2N with the total count (1.91×10¹⁰) is a 7% overestimate and may appear only labelled as one. Weights: bf16 19.10 GB; int8 9.55 GB; the 4-bit file is 8.305×10⁹ block weights at 4.125 bits (symmetric int4 with one fp16 scale per group of 128) = 4.28 GB, plus the embedding and output head at 8 bits = 1.25 GB, total 5.53 GB, written and used as 5.5 GB (W = 5.5×10⁹ in every formula, lab and widget). Cache: 147,456 B per token in bf16 (147 kB), 0.885 GB per 6,000-token request. Workload (the series', Module 07): 2,000 requests a day of 4,000 tokens in (a 3,000-token stable prefix of system prompt, output schema and fixed reference text, plus 1,000 tokens of hazard-log entries and the engineer's request) and 2,000 out; mean context during decode 5,000 tokens (0.737 GB of cache). Reference GPU: the '24 GB consumer card' at 1.0 TB/s (datasheet 1.008) and 165 TFLOP/s dense fp16 with fp32 accumulation (the RTX 4090's published figures); runtime overhead 2.5 GB (an assumption: say so); 16 GB of cache; 18 sequences. Decode bounds always include the sequence's cache: one sequence at a 5,000-token context reads 6.24 GB per step with the 4-bit file (160 tokens/s on the 24 GB card), 19.84 GB in bf16 (50) and 10.29 GB in int8 (97). Lab 3's simulator draws its own output lengths (lognormal, median 1,500, mean about 1,740 after the clip at 4,000) while s11 sizes for 2,000: say so wherever the two meet, and take simulator costs from its printed throughput. MODULE CONSISTENCY: these numbers were reconciled with Module 07's configuration, workload and prices; if any of them changes, recompute with Lab 1 (seconds) and Lab 3 (a minute).

ASSUMPTIONS THAT MUST BE LABELLED wherever they appear: prefill MFU 50% (this module's; Modules 07-09 assume 4×10¹⁴ FLOP/s sustained on an H100, 40% MFU); decode at peak bandwidth (s1 explains why the embedding-read and achieved-bandwidth corrections nearly cancel); runtime overhead 2.5 GB; every price, written 'USD x' (never with a dollar sign, which the page reads as maths) and labelled 'an assumption, as of 2026', one value per item across the series: the 24 GB card USD 1.00 per GPU-hour (e14 deliberately asks about a lower quote, USD 0.80, so that it does not repeat s11's numbers); an L4-class card USD 0.80 per hour; an H100 USD 2.50 per GPU-hour (Module 07's); a hosted API at USD 0.20 and 0.80 per million input and output tokens, with cached input at 10% of the input price (Module 07's); an owned card USD 2,000 over three years plus 0.45 kW at USD 0.20/kWh. Do not state any current cloud or API price as fact.

UNITS. Decimal throughout: kB = 10³ B, GB = 10⁹ B, TB/s = 10¹² B/s, TFLOP/s = 10¹² FLOP/s; say so once in s1, and in s4 that GPU memory is sold in GiB (a '24 GB' card holds 25.8×10⁹ bytes; the text treats the difference as margin). Modules 03 and 06 use binary units: where a quantity recurs, give both forms (Llama-2-7B's cache: 524,288 B, 512 KiB, per token). Hardware figures are dense (no sparsity), dated 'as of 2026', labelled as datasheet values and checked against the vendor's datasheet before publication: H100 SXM 80 GB, 3.35 TB/s, 989 TFLOP/s bf16; A100 80 GB SXM 2.039 TB/s, 312; L40S 48 GB, 0.864 TB/s, 362; L4 24 GB, 0.30 TB/s, 121; RTX 4090 24 GB, 1.008 TB/s, 165 (fp16, fp32 accumulate); M2 Ultra up to 192 GB, 0.8 TB/s.

NOTATION. N total parameters; N_matmul parameters in matrix multiplications; L layers; d model width (= n_h·d_head); n_h query heads; n_kv KV heads; d_head; b bytes per value; T sequence length; t position or context; B batch (concurrent sequences, consistent with the series' (B, T, d); never b, which is bytes per value here); W weight bytes; k (or kv) cache bytes per token; BW bandwidth; P_peak peak FLOP/s; I arithmetic intensity; α acceptance rate; γ draft length; c draft-to-target cost ratio; v verification cost in target steps (v_γ when it depends on γ); ρ utilisation; λ arrival rate. Metrics: TTFT, TPOT, ITL, E2E, p50/p99. First use 'key-value (KV) cache', then 'KV cache' or 'the cache'.

CORRECTIONS TO THE SOURCE that the text must carry silently (no 'the source says'): (1) a 24 GB L4-class card has 0.30 TB/s, so it is not a 150-180 tokens/s card for the case study (48 tokens/s); the 150-180 figure holds for a ~1 TB/s card; (2) the prefill of 4,000 tokens is about 0.9 s on a 24 GB consumer card and 0.15 s on an H100, so 'well under a second' and 'tens of milliseconds' hold only on datacentre GPUs; (3) the speed-up of speculative decoding is not 'the acceptance rate' but (1 − α^{γ+1})/((1 − α)(γc + v)); (4) PagedAttention's gain is reported as 2-4× throughput; (5) the '80 GB H100/H20-class' row becomes two rows by bandwidth; (6) throughput does not scale 'almost linearly until compute becomes the limit' at long context, because cache reads grow with the batch.

DEPARTURES FROM THE EDITOR'S SUGGESTIONS, and why. (a) Hardware is s4, before batching, so that every later section can use real numbers; cost per million tokens is derived in s11 (sizing), where the throughput it needs is computed. (b) Two widgets instead of one combined calculator: serving-calculator (s11) and speculative-speedup (s9); one widget doing both would bury the second teaching point. (c) Lab 2 defines its own compact decoder instead of importing Module 06's code, because each lab must be self-contained; it also absorbs the source's Exercise 4 (prefix caching cold and warm) as its last step on SmolLM2-135M. (d) Lab 4 goes beyond weight quantisation to activation outliers, simulated W8A8 and SmoothQuant, because the prototype showed a striking and cheap demonstration (activation channel ratio about 1,960 against 12 for weights; W8A8 perplexity 40.7 repaired to 24.6). (f) Lab 3 models hybrid iterations (a prefill chunk shares the forward pass with decodes: cost = max(bytes/BW, FLOPs/compute)), not 'prefill time added to the step'; the naive model wrongly makes chunked prefill look harmful.
